docs.text: Event Emitted Carries WorldStructureChangedEvent globally, when an actor is created, destroyed, moved, activated or deactivated, and when a world is loaded or unloaded worldAssetID, changeType (CREATED, DESTROYED, MOVED, ACTIVATED, DEACTIVATED, LOADED, UNLOADED), actorName TagsChangedEvent to the world (its asset id), the actor or the component (its id in the world) whose tags changed, in a loaded world. Not when a world is loaded added, removed (the explicit tags that changed). See Tags

docs.title: Input events
docs.text:
Every OS input event is also sent globally, as it is reported, during the Input phase (so before the frame's scripts run). The input state read through IInput is already up to date when a handler runs. Events carry no source object (ObjectID(0)).

Event Carries KeyPressedEvent / KeyReleasedEvent keyCode (an Input::Key, or key()), and repeated for a press made by the OS key repeat TextInputEvent text (UTF-8), layout and modifiers applied : for text fields, not for bindings MouseButtonPressedEvent / MouseButtonReleasedEvent button, x, y in the window MouseMovedEvent x, y, deltaX, deltaY (the delta is still reported while the cursor is captured) MouseScrolledEvent deltaX, deltaY GamepadConnectedEvent / GamepadDisconnectedEvent deviceId GamepadButtonPressedEvent / GamepadButtonReleasedEvent deviceId, button GamepadAxisEvent deviceId, axis, value : raw, with no dead zone, on every change 
events->subscribeGlobal<Events::KeyPressedEvent>([](const Events::KeyPressedEvent& e) {
    if (e.key() == Input::Key::E && !e.repeated)
        Interact();
});

Use the events to react to a change (a press, a plug), and the polled state (IsKeyDown, GetGamepadAxis, ...) for what is held. Deterministic runs and replays emit them too, as they come from the same OS events.

docs.title: Script callbacks are not dispatcher events
docs.text:
The contact events of physics (ContactAddedEvent, ContactPersistedEvent, ContactRemovedEvent, in engine/physics/physics_events.hpp) reuse the Event base, but they are not sent through the dispatcher : they are handed straight to the scripts of the actors involved, as the OnContactAdded, OnContactPersisted and OnContactEnded overrides of Script. They are delivered after the physics step, on the thread that ran it ; a script may read and change bodies, or destroy actors, there.

The other lifecycle hooks of a script (OnCreate, OnPlay, OnTick, OnStop, OnActivated, OnDeactivated, OnDestroyed, OnWorldLoaded, OnWorldUnloaded) are plain virtual calls too. Use the dispatcher when the sender and the receiver do not know each other ; use the callbacks for what concerns the script's own actor.

See also : Time for when in the frame each of these runs.

docs.title: Gravity fields
docs.text:
How to change which way, and how hard, bodies fall in a region of the world.

Jolt has one gravity for the whole simulation (physics.gravity in the project settings). Gravity fields and the per-body gravity are done on top of it : before every step, each awake dynamic body is given as a force the difference between the gravity it should feel and the one Jolt is about to give it. A project without fields, with every body on the default mode, pays nothing for it.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text:
All of them are components with a strength (acceleration, in world units per second squared, 9.81 for the Earth in a project in metres, negative pushes away), a priority and a blend.

Component Type name What it does UniformGravityField gravityUniform The same gravity everywhere : a direction (down by default) turned by the rotation of its actor. A level's own gravity. PointGravityField gravityPoint Pulls toward its actor, with a radius (0 : unlimited) and a falloff : Constant, Linear (to nothing at the radius) or InverseSquare (strength is reached at referenceDistance, and stops growing under minDistance). RadialGravityField gravityRadial A planet : strength is the gravity of the surface at radius. Above it falls by falloff (inverse square by default) up to reach (0 : unlimited). Inside, it decreases to the center like a ball of uniform density (solidInterior) or stays constant. GravityVolume gravityVolume A region (the box of its actor, or the sphere / cylinder inscribed in it, following its position, rotation and scale) where gravity is something else. It points Fixed (along direction), ToCenter or ToAxis (the Y axis : a rotating station, with a negative strength). Fades in over fadeDistance inside its edge.

Point, radial and volume fields fade to nothing at their edge when given a fadeDistance, so a body crossing it feels the change gradually.

docs.title: Combining them
docs.text:
The fields that cover a position are read from the highest priority to the lowest :

  • an Override field replaces what is below it, over the share of the position it covers (1 deep inside, less near a fading edge) ;
  • overriding fields of the same priority that overlap blend, by their coverage ;
  • what no field covers is the lower fields', and at last the project's gravity ;
  • an Additive field is summed on top of the result, whatever its priority (a moon pulling over a planet's gravity).

A body on the far side of a planet falls toward its center, and a body walking from a planet's field into a corridor volume of a higher priority sees its gravity turn over the corridor's fade.

docs.title: Per-body gravity
docs.text:
PhysicsBody has a gravityMode :

Mode The body feels Fields (default) the project's gravity, changed by the fields where its center of mass is World the project's gravity alone, the fields do not touch it Custom its own customGravity

The gravityFactor scales whatever the gravity is (0 floats, negative falls up).

auto body = actor->GetComponent<PhysicsBody>();

body->SetCustomGravity(glm::vec3(0, 3, 0));         // gravityMode = Custom
body->SetGravityMode(GravityMode::Fields);          // back to the world's

glm::vec3 g = body->GetGravity();                   // what it falls with now, gravity factor included
glm::vec3 up = -glm::normalize(g);                  // the "up" of a character standing on a planet

PhysicsManager::GetGravityAt(position) gives the gravity of the fields and the world at any point of the root frame, for what is not a body (a camera, a particle, an AI).

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Fields are read in the root frame, in double, like Jolt : a planet 10^12 m from the origin works (see Large world).
  • Fields are read again for every fixed step : move them, turn them, change their fields from a script.
  • A sleeping body is woken when a change of the fields changes the gravity it would feel (a field appearing, going away, moving), and left alone otherwise. A body whose component is deactivated is never woken.
  • The kinematic and static bodies ignore gravity, as always.
  • The simulation does not depend on the order the components were added in : a tie between two fields of the same priority is broken by their order in the world.
  • PhysicsManager::SetGravityFields takes the fields as plain numbers (GravityFieldData), for tests or for code that has no component to give.

docs.title: Headless mode and determinism
docs.text:
A project's simulation can run with no window, GPU or sound card, and it can be made deterministic: the same inputs and seed give the same state on every frame, on Windows and Linux. This is used for:

  • dedicated servers that run the simulation without rendering
  • simulation regression tests in CI, replaying a recorded run and checking its state along the way
  • replays, since a session's inputs take only a few KB
ShardHeadless --game plugins/game/bin/windows-x86_64/libGameModule.dll --project example_project.json --replay run.replay

docs.title: ShardHeadless
docs.text:
ShardHeadless (src/apps/headless) is the player without a screen: same engine, same game module, same simulation code. It uses the headless platform (a fake window that only has a size and an event queue, SDL is never initialized) and the null graphics backend.

Option --game <module> --project <file> game module and project (required) --world <path> world to load (default: the replay's, otherwise the project's first world) --frames <n> number of frames to run (default: replay length, otherwise 600) --seed <n\|random> seed for the random streams (default: the replay's, otherwise 1) --replay <file> plays back a replay, feeding its inputs to the game and verifying its state checks --write-replay <file> records this run to a replay. Use it to create one, or to update the checks after a change that is meant to affect the simulation --check-every <n> adds a state check every n frames (default 60) --expect <hash> expected state hash after the last frame --require-checks with --replay, fails if the replay has no checks --print-state prints the full state at each check --script <file> runs console commands at given frames, one <frame> <command> per line (e.g. 60 sim.hash prints the state hash and seed) --server runs in real time at the fixed step until stopped, as a dedicated server

Exit codes: 0 success (and matched), 1 failed to start, 2 diverged. The last line of output is [HEADLESS] state <hash> frames <n> ..., which is easy to parse from a script.

--server runs the same loop as everywhere else, except that it sleeps until the next fixed step instead of running as fast as it can.

docs.title: Null graphics backend
docs.text:
RendererAPI::API::Null (renderer/rhi/backends/null) implements the whole RHI without drawing anything. Meshes keep their geometry, textures their specs, materials their parameters, and framebuffers have a size and read back as black. The rest of the frame still runs (extraction, culling, pass setup, draw lists), so the CPU side of the renderer is exercised in headless runs and in tests/rendering/null_rhi_tests.cpp without a GPU.

This backend has no separate graphics thread. Everything runs on the calling thread.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text:
EngineCreationSettings::deterministic makes runs reproducible. It is always on in ShardHeadless, and in the player with --record or --replay.

What How Fixed timestep Each frame is exactly one fixed step and the clock is never read. One Run is one physics step, and GetDeltaTime() returns the fixed step. Stable system order The scheduler runs systems within a phase in registration order, whatever the thread count (see scheduler.hpp). Scripts and physics bodies are kept in ordered maps, so they update in insertion order and not hash table order. Seeded RNG All random streams derive from one seed (--seed, saved in the replay). GetEngine().MakeRandomStream("name") gives a system its own PCG32 generator (integer-only, so identical on every platform). A given name always yields the same sequence for a given seed, whatever order systems start in. GUIDs are generated from the seed instead of the OS. Don't use rand(), std::random_device or std::uniform_*_distribution in anything that affects the simulation, since implementations differ between standard libraries. Jolt deterministic mode Jolt is built with CROSS_PLATFORM_DETERMINISTIC (CMake option SHARD_DETERMINISTIC_PHYSICS, on by default), which disables FMA and uses its own sin/cos. We also pass -ffp-contract=off so the compiler doesn't fuse a * b + c on its own. Physics runs on one thread in deterministic mode: Jolt's results don't depend on thread count, but the order of contact callbacks does, and so does whatever scripts do in them. No outside interference Hot reload is disabled. There is no window, so no resize or focus events unless the replay contains them.

A game that wants replay support has to follow the same rules: use MakeRandomStream for randomness, GetDeltaTime() or the fixed step for time, and avoid sin, cos, pow and similar on anything that ends up in the state (the last bit can differ between C libraries). Core::Random uses none of them (OnUnitSphere and OnUnitCircle use rejection sampling).

docs.title: State hash
docs.text: HashSimulationState (src/engine/simulation_state.hpp) reduces the simulation state to 64 bits. For each world it hashes every actor's transform, the pose and velocities of every physics body (as stored by Jolt), and every reflected field of every script, read-only ones included since they hold runtime state. Everything is visited by id, never in hash table order, and floats are hashed by their raw bits (Determinism::StateHasher), so one flipped bit changes the result. The hash has three parts (transforms, physics, scripts), so when a run diverges you know where to look.

docs.title: Replays
docs.text:
A replay (platform/replay/input_replay.hpp) is a text file holding the seed, fixed step, world, per-frame inputs and state checks ("after 60 frames the hash should be X").

shard-replay 1
seed 1
fixed-step #3c888889
world determinism.world
frames 600
check 60 bf7eabc5c5ff73f9 440e665432c876d0 c05a9388c8b98a39 890e766995745921
@20 key-down W
@120 key-up W
@400 mouse-move #43c80000 #42c80000 #40000000 #00000000

Keys are stored by name, so reordering the enum doesn't break old replays. Floats are stored as bit patterns and read back exactly. Replays can be edited by hand: decimal values work, and # starts a comment. Events for frame F are delivered just before frame F runs, so that frame's scripts see them.

To record, run ShardGame --record run.replay. It saves keyboard, mouse and gamepad input, plus a state check every --check-every frames (60 by default). The run is deterministic while recording.

To play it back, use ShardGame --replay run.replay to watch it (keyboard input is ignored), or ShardHeadless --replay run.replay to check it without a window. Both give the same hashes, because the graphics backend and the window don't affect the simulation.

docs.title: Regression test
docs.text:
tests/determinism holds a small project (a floor, a wall, some bodies that fall and get kicked at random by RandomKicker scripts, and a keyboard-controlled Character, all of them scripts of the example game, which is written with the SDK) and a replay (golden/determinism.replay) that walks around with WASD for 600 frames. CTest runs it through ShardHeadless as Determinism.Replay. CI runs it on Windows and Linux on runners without a GPU, and fails if any check doesn't match:

[REPLAY FAILED] the run diverged from the replay after 60 frames : expected state bf7eabc5c5ff73f9, got 5e47b74a8a3edcc4 (differs : transforms)

If a change is meant to affect the simulation (different physics settings, a new script field...), re-record the replay and commit it:

ShardHeadless --game build/plugins/game/bin/windows-x86_64/libGameModule.dll --project tests/determinism/project/determinism_project.json \
              --replay tests/determinism/golden/determinism.replay --write-replay tests/determinism/golden/determinism.replay

If it passes on one platform and fails on the other, something in the simulation depends on the platform: a sin/cos in the state, iteration over a hash table, uninitialized memory, a clock read. The three parts of the hash show which state to look at.

docs.title: Large world
docs.text: How Shard keeps positions exact from a room to a solar system.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A float has 24 bits of mantissa : 10 km from the origin the smallest step is ~1 mm, at 100 km it is ~8 mm and things jitter. A double is exact to a micrometre over the solar system, but the GPU wants floats. The rule is :

Big numbers live in the frames' origins and in integers. Everything else is small.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text: Piece Where What it is WorldPosition core/math/large_world.hpp (CellCoord cell, dvec3 local) : an int64 cell of 1024 m plus a double offset inside it. a - b is exact when a and b are near each other, however far from the origin they are. ReferenceFrameTree core/math/reference_frame.hpp Nested frames (floating origins : a planet, a ship, a streaming cell). Each frame has an origin (WorldPosition) and a rotation in its parent. Converts points, directions and rotations between any two frames, through their nearest common ancestor. World::GetFrames() world/world.hpp Every world owns a tree. It is saved in the world file ("frames"). Transform::frame world/components/transform.hpp The frame an actor hierarchy lives in (set on the root actor). position stays a small float in that frame. Jolt in double CMakeLists.txt SHARD_DOUBLE_PRECISION_PHYSICS (ON) builds Jolt with JPH_DOUBLE_PRECISION : bodies are positioned in the root frame in double. Extract renderer/components/render_extractor.cpp Turns everything into camera-relative floats. The renderer is unchanged.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
auto& frames = world.GetFrames();
FrameId planet = frames.Create("Planet", kRootFrame,
                               WorldPosition(CellCoord{1000000000, 0, 0}, dvec3(0)));   // ~10^12 m from the root

actor->transform->frame = planet;               // a root actor of the hierarchy
actor->transform->SetPosition({0, 2, 0});       // small, in the planet's frame

WorldPosition where = actor->transform->GetWorldCoords();   // exact, in the root frame
dvec3 p = actor->transform->GetWorldPositionD();            // the same, collapsed to a double
actor->transform->SetWorldCoords(frames.ToRoot(planet, dvec3(10, 0, -4)));

dvec3 q = frames.ConvertPoint(shipFrame, planetFrame, dvec3(1, 2, 3));   // frame -> frame

ConvertPoint between two frames that are far from the root but near each other keeps the precision of their small distance : the two legs of the conversion are carried as WorldPositions and only the exact difference is narrowed.

docs.title: Physics
docs.text:
Jolt simulates in the root frame, in double. A PhysicsBody is created at Transform::GetWorldPositionD() / GetWorldRotationD() and, after every step, its result is brought back into the actor's frame (RootToFramePosition), so the transform, the pose interpolation and the world matrix keep working with small floats. Velocities, sizes and forces stay float. PhysicsBody::GetPositionD / SetPositionD are the double accessors.

Frames are assumed static while their bodies are simulated (moving a frame does not move the bodies already in Jolt : teleport them with SetPositionD).

Changing the Jolt precision changes the simulation : tests/determinism/golden/determinism.replay was recorded again with this change.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
The Extract stage picks a render origin, a WorldPosition of the root frame that follows the camera. Every position, matrix and view put in the RenderSnapshot is a float relative to it (FrameToRender, render_space.hpp : the subtraction is done in double, on exact positions, before the narrowing). The renderer only sees small numbers and does not know any of this.

  • The origin moves (to a cell corner under the camera) only when the camera is farther than render.rebase_distance from it (default 4096 m, 0 = always exactly at the camera). In a scene that fits within that distance the origin never moves, render space is the root frame, and extraction gives the very same matrices as before (bit for bit).
  • When it moves, RenderSnapshot::originShift is where the previous origin is seen from the new one : something that stores a render-space position from one frame to the next (temporal history) adds it. Every proxy is flagged changed that frame.
  • Not yet covered : the orientation of probe volumes in a rotated frame (their boxes stay axis-aligned), and the editor's picking / gizmos, which still work in the actor's frame (identical to the render space as long as the origin has not moved).

docs.title: Baked lighting (lightmaps)
docs.text:
A lightmap stores the diffuse light reaching a surface: sky light, the lights you choose to bake, and the light bouncing between surfaces. It is computed once with the engine's path tracer and saved in a texture mapped onto the surface. At runtime the forward pass only samples it. This gives soft, noise-free shadows, color bleeding and ambient occlusion at a few centimeters per texel, at no per-frame cost.

Lightmaps work next to the real-time GI probes and don't replace them. Moving models are still lit by the probes, and baked models still take their reflections from them.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Mark static objects. Every model has a Static Lighting option, on by default. Static models block and bounce light during the bake and get a lightmap. Turn it off for anything that moves: a baked shadow won't follow the object, and its lightmap would stay where it was baked. Non-static models are lit by the probes and the real-time lights.

  2. Set the light modes. Every light has a Bake Mode:

    Mode Direct light Bounced light Use it for Dynamic (default) real-time not baked lights that move or change Stationary real-time (shadow maps, specular highlights) baked lights that stay put but need highlights or runtime tweaks Static baked (not computed at runtime on lightmapped surfaces) baked the main lights of the scene; cheapest and best-looking

    Static lights are still applied in real time on surfaces without a lightmap (moving models), so both match.

    A Dynamic light bounces nowhere on lightmapped surfaces: the lightmap only holds the sky and the baked lights. For a sun that doesn't move, use Stationary, or its bounce light is missing (raising Indirect intensity to make up for it brightens the sky light everywhere instead).

    Source Size gives a light a physical size: the lamp radius in world units for point and spot lights, or the sun disc's angular radius in degrees for directional lights (the real sun is 0.27). Larger sources give softer shadows in the baker and the offline raytracer. Real-time shadow maps ignore it.

  3. Bake. Go to World Settings > Rendering > Lightmaps > Bake, or run lightmaps.bake in the console. The bake is spread over several frames with a progress notification, so the editor stays usable. Save the world when it finishes: the world file stores each model's lightmap location, and the pages are written to lightmaps/<world>.lightmap in the project.

  4. Iterate. After changing a light or moving a static model, press Re-bake. Delete removes the lightmaps and goes back to probe lighting.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Texels per meter Lightmap resolution, the same for every model. About 8 gives soft light on large surfaces, 32 gives sharp shadow edges, 64 or more suits hero props. Samples Paths traced per texel. 256 looks clean, use 1024 or more for final quality. Bounces 1 means only sky light and the direct light of Static lights. Each extra bounce adds light reflected between surfaces. Indirect intensity Multiplies everything except the direct light of Static lights, like Unreal's "indirect lighting intensity". 1 is physically correct, 2 to 4 brightens the shadows for a flatter look. Denoise Edge-aware filter using the surface data and each texel's noise level. It smooths flat areas and keeps shadow edges sharp. Denoiser settings Under Denoise. Passes (each one doubles the filter's reach), Light tolerance (how much light difference still counts as noise; higher is smoother but blurs soft shadows), Normal sharpness (how fast surfaces facing different ways stop mixing) and Plane tolerance (how far from the surface's plane a neighbour may be, in texels). Applied at the next bake. Firefly clamp Caps how bright a single path can be, so rare very bright samples don't show up as white dots. In addition, before denoising, a texel more than 2.5 times brighter than its brightest neighbour is brought down to that limit : a lone bright dot is a spike, a real edge of light always has a bright neighbour. If dots remain in a dark scene, lower the clamp (4 to 8). Max page size, max resolution per model Lightmaps are packed into pages (textures) no larger than this, at 4 bytes per texel, and no model goes above the max resolution. You can also override the resolution per model with Lightmap Resolution.

Settings are saved in the world file, so the next bake reuses them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Lightmap UVs. When a mesh loads, it gets a second UV set (mesh.lightmap_uvs). The surface is split into charts of triangles facing roughly the same way, each chart is flattened, and all of them are packed at the same scale so texel density is uniform. The process is deterministic and cached in <project>/.cache/lightmap_uv (safe to delete), so a huge mesh is only unwrapped once.
  • Layout. Each static model gets a lightmap size from the texel density, and they are all packed into an atlas (PlanLightmapLayout).
  • Baking. The CPU rasterizes each page into a G-buffer holding the position and normal of every texel. The GPU then traces paths from each texel (lightmap_bake.comp, which shares its path tracer with the offline raytracer): one cosine-weighted path for indirect light, and one shadow ray per Static light toward a random point on its emitter. The paths go through the back faces of single-sided materials, as the raster culls them (set Double Sided on the material if a surface should be seen from behind). Shadow rays stop on both faces, like the sun's shadow maps with the project's Double-sided Casters. The results become a mean and a variance (lightmap_resolve.comp), then are denoised with five iterations of an à-trous filter (lightmap_atrous.comp). Finally the page is read back, its gutters are filled so bilinear filtering never picks up black at chart edges, and it is packed into shared-exponent texels.
  • Runtime. lit.frag samples the page through a bindless handle (all sampler units are already taken) and uses it in place of the diffuse light from the probes and the sky. Pages are stored as GL_RGB9_E5, half the size of RGBA16F and without banding on smooth gradients.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
Command lightmaps.bake [samples] [texels per meter] [bounces] [max page size] [max resolution] bakes the static models of the first world lightmaps.status shows the current bake and the lightmaps used by the world lightmaps.clear deletes the baked lightmaps world.save saves the first world to its file raytrace.render <file.hdr> [width] [height] [samples] [bounces] [terms] path traces the world from the active camera to a linear HDR file, plus a .png preview ; terms also writes the light split by term (see the renderer's Comparing against the path tracer)

The mesh.lightmap_uvs console variable (on by default) turns off lightmap UV generation. Meshes loaded without them fall back to probe lighting.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Diffuse only. Specular highlights from Static lights aren't baked (use Stationary if you need them), and reflections still come from the probes and the skybox.
  • Baked lighting doesn't follow changes to lights or geometry until you bake again. It also ignores normal maps, since it stores the light received by a flat surface.
  • A page uses size² × 4 bytes of VRAM, and baking needs about size² × 80 bytes while a page is traced. A level made of one giant mesh (the Sponza sample has 5.7 million triangles) needs a 4096 page. Splitting a level into many static meshes gives sharper results for the same cost.
  • Static models need lightmap UVs, and the world must be loaded before baking. The bake builds its BVH on the engine's job system, so avoid baking a big scene while physics runs (play mode).

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module is a part of a Shard project that brings components, systems and content, and follows the lifecycle of the worlds. The engine itself is made of modules, the genre toolkits (voxel, planetary, racing...) are modules, and so is your game. They all register what they add through the same API, so a feature written inside the engine and one written in a game look the same to the rest of the code.

Modules are plugins : they have a manifest, dependencies, a load order, and can be enabled, disabled and reloaded. This page is about what is specific to modules.

docs.title: What the engine is made of
docs.text:
Run plugin.list in the console (or open the Plugins window in the editor) :

#   id                                version     kind      state       tier ms/frame  notes
1   shard.assets                      0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
2   shard.audio                       0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
3   shard.core                        0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
4   shard.physics                     0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
5   shard.renderer                    0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
6   shard.world                       0.1.0       engine    Enabled     0    0.00      static
7   game                              0.0.0       code      Enabled     0    0.00      sim

The shard.* entries are the engine's own modules. They are compiled into the executable and always load first, so a plugin can depend on them ("dependencies": ["shard.physics"]) to say what it builds on. They cannot be disabled.

The game library you pass with --game is the module game.

docs.title: What a module can do
docs.text: Add components and systems ctx.Components(), ctx.Systems(). Systems join the schedule with the same reads / writes as the engine's, and run in plugin load order Follow the worlds OnWorldLoaded, OnWorldUnloaded, OnPlayStart, OnPlayStop are called for every world Carry content files mounted as mod://<id>/, layered over each other, with tables and translations merged Patch worlds datapacks change a world file as it is read Provide services an interface other modules ask for by name and version Declare components a datapack can describe a component made of fields, which then behaves like any other

docs.title: Rules between modules
docs.text:
• A module reaches another one through components, events or services, not through its headers.
  • A genre module or a game module includes the public headers only. python scripts/check_deps.py checks the layering in CI.
  • A module that draws gets the frame's snapshot, never the world.

See Plugins and modules for the manifest, the API, the build and the datapack formats.

docs.title: Platform Abstraction Layer (PAL)
docs.text:
src/engine/platform/ is the only code that talks to the OS or the window system. It depends on ShardCore and SDL3 and nothing else. The layers above go through its API, and scripts/check_deps.py fails CI if an OS or SDL header appears elsewhere in src/engine/.

Each module has a public header with no OS types, and one implementation file per OS (*_win32.cpp / *_posix.cpp, chosen with #if).

Folder Contents windowing/ IWindow, IPlatform; SDL3 backend (SDLWindow, SDLPlatform<T>): GL context, monitors, DPI, HDR, fullscreen events/ OSEvent: typed window system events, with several listeners per window devices/ IInput (keyboard, mouse, gamepads), Key, GamepadButton, GamepadAxis; SDL3 backend clipboard/ Clipboard text, file / folder / message dialogs filesystem/ Paths (user directories), FileWatcher (ReadDirectoryChangesW / inotify), AsyncIO (IOCP / io_uring / thread pool) lib_loader/ DynLib, ModuleLoader thread/, atomic/, time/ Named, prioritised and pinned threads, HardwareConcurrency(), SpinLock, NowNanoseconds(), PreciseSleep() process/ Environment, executable path, Process::Launch, reveal in file manager crash/ Crash report and minidump, crash hooks, Ctrl+C / SIGTERM handler network/ Socket (UDP / TCP), NamedPipe, SharedMemory hardware/ CPU features, RAM, OS, per-process memory (CPU and GPU)

docs.title: Building on Linux
docs.text: SDL3 is built from source, so you need the development packages for your window system (X11 / Wayland, ALSA / PulseAudio, libudev...). liburing-dev is optional. With it, async IO uses io_uring when the kernel allows it. Without it, a small thread pool does the job. AsyncIO::BackendName() tells you which one is active.

docs.title: Gamepads
docs.text:
Pads are numbered in the order they were plugged in.

auto* input = GetEngine().GetInputManager();
if (input->GetGamepadCount() > 0) {
    float x = input->GetGamepadAxis(0, Input::GamepadAxis::LeftX);   // dead zone applied
    if (input->WasGamepadButtonPressed(0, Input::GamepadButton::South))
        input->SetGamepadRumble(0, 0.5f, 0.5f, 200);
}

docs.title: Plugins and modules
docs.text:
How to extend Shard without changing the engine : game code, genre toolkits, mods, datapacks, editor tools, server add-ons.

Everything that extends Shard is a plugin. A module is a plugin that also carries game content (components, assets, worlds). The engine's own parts (physics, audio, renderer...) show up in the same list as modules, and the game is a module too, so a plugin can depend on any of them the same way.

The code lives in src/engine/plugins/. Plugins::PluginManager (manager.hpp) finds, checks, loads, runs and unloads the plugins of an executable.

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text:
Kind Loaded by Typical use EnginePlugin the editor, the player, ShardHeadless render features, importers, extensions of physics or audio, per-frame work EditorPlugin the editor only windows, inspectors, editor commands ServerPlugin ShardHeadless accepting or refusing clients, administration, metrics ToolPlugin the offline tools (ShardAssetValidator) checks for the asset validator, tasks the tools run IModule wherever its manifest says game code, genre modules, mods, datapacks

IModule derives from IPlugin, so a module has everything a plugin has (manifest, lifecycle, dependencies, registration context) plus content : a file tree mounted as mod://<id>/, and callbacks that follow the worlds.

Module kinds :

Module kind Contains Runs code engine a part of the engine itself (shard.physics, shard.audio...) yes, compiled into the executable genre a reusable toolkit : voxel, planetary, racing... yes, native code a game's own C++ yes, native mod content and logic made by someone else yes, native datapack worlds, prefabs, data tables, translations no

A plugin lists the hosts it can run in. A host only loads the plugins that name it, so editor code never ends up in a shipped player.

docs.title: Installing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin is a folder with a shard-plugin.json at its root, or the same folder packed in a .shardplugin archive (a ZIP file : see Packaging). Put it in the project's plugins folder (pluginsFolder in the project file, shown under Project Settings > Plugins), or in any folder listed in the SHARD_PLUGIN_PATH environment variable (separated by :, or ; on Windows). Shard looks at that folder, and one level of subfolders below it, for plugin folders and .shardplugin archives. An archive is unpacked once into a cache folder (.cache/plugin_cache next to the project) named after its hash, then loaded from there.

The project file can then say which plugins it wants :

"plugins": [
  { "id": "com.acme.weather", "version": "^1.4", "required": true,
    "settings": { "rain_rate": 0.4 } },
  { "id": "com.acme.clouds", "enabled": false },
  { "id": "my.local.mod", "path": "mods/local" }
]
Key Meaning id the plugin version a version range ; when several versions of the plugin are found, the highest one inside it is used, and a plugin that does not fit is refused enabled false leaves the plugin out required the project cannot run without it : if it cannot be loaded, startup stops with the reason path a plugin folder or a .shardplugin archive, relative to the project, in addition to the plugins folder allowUnsigned load this plugin even if it is a native plugin (tier 1) with no signature from a trusted publisher, see Trust levels settings values for the plugin's console variables. A key is relative to the plugin's variables (rain_rate is com.acme.weather.rain_rate)

The project file can also list "registries", the places plugin.search and plugin.install look in (see below).

A plugin the project does not mention is loaded anyway if it sits in a plugins folder. List it only to configure it, turn it off, or require it.

On the first run Shard writes plugins.lock next to the project file : the exact version and a hash of the content of every plugin that was loaded. Commit it. On later runs a difference (another version, another content, a plugin that appeared or vanished) is written to the log, and --strict-plugin-lock makes it an error. ShardHeadless and the player are strict when they play a replay. Rewrite the lock with the Write plugins.lock button of the Plugins panel, or plugin.lock write in the console. A read-only run (--frames, a replay) never writes it.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
The editor, the player and ShardHeadless take these :

Option --plugin <path> a plugin folder, a shard-plugin.json, or a library ; repeatable --plugin-path <dir> a folder that holds plugins ; repeatable --disable-plugin <id> leave a plugin out of this run ; repeatable --hot-reload-plugins player : allow plugin.reload (the editor always allows it ; a deterministic run never does) --strict-plugin-lock a plugins.lock that does not match is an error --ignore-safe-mode load a plugin even if the last run crashed in it --registry <source> a registry for plugin.search and plugin.install : an index.json, a folder holding one, or an http:// URL ; repeatable (SHARD_PLUGIN_REGISTRY adds one) --trust-file <path> a file of trusted publishers ; repeatable (default : plugin-trust.json next to the project) --allow-unsigned-plugins load native plugins and install from registries without a signature of a trusted publisher

--game <library> still works : the library is loaded as the plugin game, a code module. It does not need a manifest, and it may be a C++ plugin or one built with the SDK (the engine tells them apart by the entry point they export). The example game is built with shard_add_plugin (id game, ABI c1, so against the SDK alone), and sits at <build>/plugins/game/bin/<platform>/ with its shard-plugin.json : pass the library to --game, or the folder to --plugin to load it through its manifest. Its scripts are the components game.Character, game.Gun and game.RandomKicker, as every script is named after its plugin.

ShardHeadless also has :

Option --list-plugins load the plugins, print them, exit --validate-plugin <folder> check the manifest and the content of a folder without loading anything ; exit code 1 on problems --check-plugins run the simulation twice, in two processes, with one job thread and with several, and compare the final state and the plugin set : exit code 2 if a plugin (or the engine) makes the simulation depend on the thread count --state-out <file> write the final state hash and the plugin set hash to a file --port <n> with --server : answer the plugin handshake of clients, see Determinism and multiplayer --offer-datapacks with --port : clients that lack a datapack can download it --check-server <host:port> ask a server whether the plugins loaded here are accepted, print its answer and exit (0 accepted, 3 refused)

SHARD_JOB_THREADS=<n> pins the number of job threads of any executable.

docs.title: Safe mode
docs.text: If the process crashes while plugin code runs or loads, the crash handler notes which plugin it was in .cache/plugin_safe_mode.json next to the project. The next run leaves that plugin out and says so in the log. The note is used once : the run after that tries the plugin again.

docs.title: The manifest
docs.text:
{
  "schema": 1,
  "id": "com.acme.weather",
  "name": "Weather System",
  "version": "1.4.2",
  "kind": "module",
  "moduleKind": "mod",
  "linkage": "dynamic",
  "hosts": ["engine", "tool"],

  "engine": { "api": "1.0", "versions": ">=0.1.0 <0.3.0", "requires": ["largeWorld"] },

  "binaries": {
    "linux-x86_64":   "bin/linux-x86_64/libweather.so",
    "windows-x86_64": "bin/windows-x86_64/weather.dll"
  },

  "dependencies": [
    "shard.audio",
    { "id": "com.acme.clouds", "version": "^2.1", "optional": true },
    { "id": "service:weather.query" }
  ],
  "conflicts": [ { "id": "com.other.weather" } ],
  "provides": [ { "service": "weather.query", "version": "1.0" } ],
  "loadAfter": [ "com.acme.clouds" ],

  "simulation": { "affects": true, "deterministic": true },
  "content": { "mount": "content", "assetNamespace": "acme.weather", "overrides": ["materials/*"] },
  "budgets": { "frameMs": 1.5 },
  "permissions": ["render.feature"],
  "settings": { "rain_rate": 0.2 }
}
Field Meaning id lowercase letters, digits, - and _, in dot separated segments. Never changes. Prefixes the plugin's systems (<id>/name) and console variables (<id>.name) version semantic version major.minor.patch kind, moduleKind plugin or module ; for a module engine, genre, code (the default), mod or datapack linkage static for what is compiled into the executable, dynamic (default) for a library on disk tier 0 first-party, 1 native third-party, 2 sandboxed (a WebAssembly module, "abi": "wasm1", experimental), 3 datapack. Defaults to 0 for code, 3 for a datapack hosts engine (= editor, player and headless), editor, player, headless, tool engine.api the plugin API it was built against. Refused if the major differs or the minor is above the engine's engine.versions engine versions it works with engine.requires engine features it needs : largeWorld, determinism, headless, editor, physics, audio, renderer abi how the library talks to the engine : cpp (default) for a plugin that links the engine, c1 for a plugin built with the SDK, wasm1 for a sandboxed WebAssembly module (its binary is "binaries": { "wasm": "plugin.wasm" }, the same file on every platform). shard_sdk_add_plugin and shard_add_plugin(... ABI c1) write it for you abiFingerprint optional, cpp plugins only : the build it expects (see Building). A c1 plugin is not checked against the build fingerprint binaries, entry the library per platform (linux-x86_64, windows-x86_64, macos-arm64...), and its entry point (shard_plugin_describe for cpp, shard_plugin_entry for c1) dependencies, conflicts other plugins by id and version range ; optional for a dependency that may be absent. service:<name> stands for any plugin that provides that service provides services it offers loadAfter, loadBefore ordering hints between plugins simulation.affects true if the plugin changes what the simulation computes. Defaults to true for modules content mount : the folder (inside the plugin) of its content ; assetNamespace : defaults to the id ; overrides : paths of lower layers it replaces (* for any, folder/* for a folder) budgets frameMs : milliseconds per frame it should stay under. memoryMB : megabytes of counted memory (PluginContext::Memory(), see below), and enforce : an allocation that would pass it fails instead of only being reported. A plugin over its budget is reported in the log and plugin.budgets permissions what it says it will do (fs.read:content, render.feature, net...). Read by PluginContext::Has, not enforced : see Trust levels settings defaults for its console variables (key relative to the plugin's variables), applied below the project's values tags the tags it declares ({ "Weather.Rain": { "comment": "..." } }, or an array of names) : in the tree while the plugin is loaded, shown but not editable in Project settings > Tags. See Tags

A datapack has the same manifest with moduleKind: "datapack", tier: 3 and no binaries.

ShardHeadless --validate-plugin <folder> reports every problem of a manifest at once.

docs.title: How plugins start and stop
docs.text:
Resolved > Loaded > Initialized > Enabled <> Disabled > Unloaded
                                     \
                                    Failed

At startup, before the engine initializes, the manager :

  1. Reads the manifests of the plugins folders, the project's path entries, SHARD_PLUGIN_PATH and --plugin. A broken manifest is reported and skipped.
  2. Drops what does not fit : another host, engine version, plugin API, engine feature, platform, a project that turned it off. Keeps one version per id. Drops plugins whose dependencies cannot be met (and, one after the other, what depended on them), and one side of each conflict (the id that sorts last, unless the project requires it).
  3. Fixes the load order : the engine's own modules first, then dependencies and loadAfter / loadBefore, ties broken by id. The order never depends on how the files were listed.
  4. Loads the libraries, then calls OnLoad on every plugin in that order, then OnInitialize on every plugin.
  5. Mounts the content of the modules and calls OnContentMounted.

Then the engine builds its systems, the plugins' systems and subscriptions join the schedule, and OnEnable runs on every plugin just before the first world loads. On the way out, OnDisable runs in reverse order, everything the plugins registered is removed, and the libraries are unloaded.

A plugin that throws, or cannot load, becomes Failed with the reason (see plugin.info), along with the plugins that depend on it. The engine keeps running, unless the plugin is required by the project.

Disabling a plugin (plugin.disable <id>, the Plugins panel) stops it and the plugins that depend on it, and removes everything it registered : systems, subscriptions, components, variables, commands, services, hooks, content. Its library stays loaded. Enabling it runs OnLoad, OnInitialize and OnEnable again, on the same object. A failed plugin is started over from its files. While a world is loaded, a plugin that adds components cannot be disabled (nor one that such a plugin depends on) : the world holds instances of them. Unload the worlds first, or use plugin.reload, which sets them aside and puts them back. The engine's own modules cannot be disabled.

A system that throws is caught ; the error is logged, and after ten of them the plugin is switched off.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin is a class deriving from the base for its kind, exported with SHARD_PLUGIN :

#include "engine/plugins/context.hpp"
#include "engine/plugins/plugin.hpp"

using namespace Shard::Engine;
using namespace Shard::Engine::Plugins;

class AtomShooter final : public IModule {
public:
    ModuleKind Kind() const override { return ModuleKind::Code; }

    void OnLoad(PluginContext& ctx) override {
        ctx.Components().Register<GunComponent>("game/Gun");

        Core::Ecs::SystemDesc fire;
        fire.name = "fire";
        fire.phase = Core::Ecs::Phase::Fixed;
        fire.Reads<Transform>().Writes<GunComponent>();
        fire.run = [](Core::Ecs::SystemContext& s) { /* ... */ };
        ctx.Systems().Add(std::move(fire));

        ctx.Events().Subscribe<Events::KeyPressedEvent>(
            [this](const Events::KeyPressedEvent& e) { /* ... */ });

        m_FireRate = ctx.CVars().Float("fire_rate", 8.0f, "Shots per second");
    }

private:
    Core::CVar<float>* m_FireRate = nullptr;
};

SHARD_PLUGIN(AtomShooter)

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text: Callback Called Use it to OnLoad after the library is loaded register everything : components, systems, variables, commands, services, hooks. Don't touch worlds or the GPU yet OnInitialize once every plugin has run OnLoad ask for the services of other plugins OnContentMounted (modules) the content is readable read your data tables OnEnable / OnDisable the plugin starts / stops running start or stop work of your own OnUnload right before the library is unloaded release what you own OnWorldLoaded, OnWorldUnloaded, OnPlayStart, OnPlayStop (modules) for each world, in module load order set up per-world state OnFrameBegin, OnFrameEnd (EnginePlugin) around every frame per-frame work. The time they take counts against the plugin OnEditorInit, OnEditorShutdown, OnSelectionChanged (EditorPlugin) add windows, follow the selection OnServerStart, OnServerStop, OnServerTick (ServerPlugin) ShardHeadless --server calls them at the start, after every tick and at the end OnClientConnect, OnClientDisconnect (ServerPlugin) called by whatever accepts the clients (PluginManager::NotifyClientConnect) OnClientConnect can refuse a client OnToolTask (ToolPlugin) before an offline tool runs a task refuse it with a message OnPrepareReload, OnRestore on hot reload save and restore what is not a reflected field

docs.title: The plugin context
docs.text:
Everything a plugin registers goes through its PluginContext. The context tags each registration with the plugin, so when the plugin is disabled, reloaded or unloaded the engine removes all of it. Don't call the global registries directly.

Accessor Registers Components() component types. Register<T>(name) or Register(name, factory) ; AdoptStaticRegistrars() takes the types the old REGISTER_COMPONENT macros declared in the library Systems() ECS systems, with the usual phase, Reads, Writes, After, Before. Names become <plugin id>/<name>, and ./x in After/Before means this plugin's x Events() event subscriptions (Subscribe<T>, SubscribeToWorld<T>) and Emit<T> Commands() console commands CVars() console variables, named <plugin id>.<name> : Bool, Int, Float, String. Values from the manifest and the project reach them even though they are set before the variable exists Worlds() world extensions and world settings asset references Assets() Add<T>(point, name, item) : an item for an extension point, Uri(path) and GuidOf(path) for the plugin's files Render() AddFeature and AddPipeline : items for the render.feature and render.pipeline points Hooks() interception points, see below Services() interfaces shared with other plugins, see below Content() the mounted content of all modules Memory() memory taken from the host's allocator and counted against budgets.memoryMB : Allocate/Free, New<T>/Delete, and PluginAllocator<T> for the standard containers. What is still allocated when the plugin unloads is reported as a leak MakeRandomStream(name) a seeded random stream of this plugin Log(), Warn(), Error() the log, tagged with the plugin id Has(permission) whether the manifest asked for it

docs.title: Extension points
docs.text:
Assets().Add and Render() publish items under a named point in the ExtensionRegistry (PluginManager::Get().Extensions()). Whoever owns the point reads its items, and an item leaves the registry (and the engine) with its plugin. These points are read by the engine :

Point Item type What the engine does with it render.feature Rendering::RenderFeature Render().AddFeature<Rendering::RenderFeature>(name, feature). Activated on the graphics thread, called with each frame's snapshot, deactivated before the plugin goes. render.features in the console lists them render.pipeline Rendering::RenderPipelineExtension Render().AddPipeline<Rendering::RenderPipelineExtension>(name, item). A new kind of pipeline that .renderpipeline assets and render.pipeline can name. If it is the one drawing when its plugin goes, the forward pipeline takes over asset.type Core::Resources::AssetTypeExtension a kind of asset with its loader and file extensions. The engine gives it a kind id (item->kind), files with its extensions are indexed as assets of the project (Filesystem::Type::T_CUSTOM), and what is cached of the kind is dropped when the plugin goes asset.importer Filesystem::AssetImporterExtension converts a source format into files the engine reads. asset.import <file> [folder] runs it, Filesystem::AssetImporters::Get().Import does from code editor.panel EditorPanelItem AddEditorPanel(ctx, "My window", draw) from OnEditorInit adds a window to the Window menu editor.menu EditorMenuItem an item of a menu of the menu bar ("Tools/Bake/All") editor.toolbar EditorToolbarItem a button in the viewport's toolbar editor.inspector EditorInspectorItem what is drawn below a component (or below all of them) in the Properties panel editor.gizmo EditorGizmoItem what is drawn in the viewport for each selected actor tool.validator ToolValidatorItem a check ShardAssetValidator runs : it gets the project file and returns the problems it found

Pass the base type explicitly when you add something that derives from it (Add<Rendering::RenderFeature>(name, std::make_shared<MyFeature>())), the engine finds items by that type. Other names can be used between plugins and engine code that agree on them.

docs.title: Drawing with ImGui
docs.text: An editor plugin that draws windows needs ImGui, and a library has its own copy of ImGui's globals. Build it with shard_add_plugin(... EDITOR_UI) (ImGui is compiled into it), include engine/plugins/editor_imgui.hpp and call BindEditorImGui(editor) first thing in OnEditorInit : it gives the library the editor's ImGui context and allocators. Its panel callbacks can then call ImGui as usual.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Events tell you something happened. A hook lets you change the outcome or cancel it :

ctx.Hooks().On<Hooks::PreWorldLoad>(Priority::Normal, [](Hooks::PreWorldLoad& h) {
    if (h.worldName == "forbidden.world")
        h.Cancel("blocked by acme.policy");
});
Hook Cancel means PreEngineInit, PostEngineInit PreWorldLoad, PostWorldLoad the start world is not loaded PrePlay, PostPlay play mode does not start PreFrame, PostFrame PreSave the world is not written AssetImported PlayerConnecting the client is refused (when the host calls NotifyClientConnect) PreShutdown

Handlers run by priority (Earliest to Latest), then in plugin load order, then in the order they were added. A handler that cancels does not stop the later ones ; they can read cancelled. Hooks are found by name (H::kName), not by C++ type, so they work between the executable and a library.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Plugins talk to each other through services instead of including each other's headers :

// provider, in OnLoad
ctx.Services().Provide<IWeatherQuery>("weather.query", 1, &m_Impl);

// consumer, in OnInitialize
m_Weather = ctx.Services().Get<IWeatherQuery>("weather.query", "^1.0");
...
if (m_Weather)
    float rain = m_Weather->RainAt(position);

A ServiceRef becomes empty when the provider is disabled or unloaded, so check it before use. Declare provides in the provider's manifest and service:<name> in the consumer's dependencies so that the load order and the resolution know about it.

docs.title: Rules to know
docs.text:
• Register in OnLoad, use other plugins in OnInitialize or later.
  • Use the engine's job system. Don't create threads : a plugin with work in flight can't be unloaded.
  • Release what you own in OnUnload. The host removes what went through the context ; anything else (GPU resources, files, your own threads) is yours.
  • Don't free what you didn't allocate. Memory that crosses between the plugin and the engine has to come from the same allocator.
  • Exceptions stay inside the plugin. The host catches them at every callback and system, but an exception can't cross a library boundary safely in general.
  • Don't read the world from a render feature. It works from the frame's snapshot.
  • Don't include engine internals from a genre or game module : the layering check (scripts/check_deps.py) enforces it.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
shard_add_plugin (cmake/ShardPlugin.cmake) creates the library and writes its manifest :

shard_add_plugin(
    NAME         weather
    ID           com.acme.weather
    VERSION      1.4.2
    KIND         module
    MODULE_KIND  mod
    HOSTS        engine
    DEPENDS      shard.audio "com.acme.clouds?@^2.1"
    ENGINE_REQUIRES largeWorld
    CONTENT_DIR  content
    SOURCES      weather.cpp
)

It lays the plugin out where the manager finds it : <build>/plugins/<id>/shard-plugin.json, bin/<platform>/<library>, and content/ when CONTENT_DIR is given. DEPENDS takes id, id@range, or id? for an optional one. AFFECTS_SIMULATION or NO_SIMULATION set simulation.affects (modules affect it by default). EDITOR_UI compiles ImGui into the library, for an editor plugin that draws windows. The library links the engine and is built with BUILD_GAME. With ABI c1 it links nothing of the engine and sees only sdk/include, which is how the example game is built.

ABI c1 builds a plugin of the C ABI instead : the library links nothing of the engine, only sees the headers of sdk/include, and its manifest says "abi": "c1". Outside the engine's repository, use shard_sdk_add_plugin from the SDK, which lays the plugin out the same way (see Write a game with the SDK).

The library exports its entry point with SHARD_PLUGIN(Class), or SHARD_PLUGIN_WITH_LINK(Class, fn) when it has to set up a copy of another library's statics (the game module does it for Jolt's allocator). A library does not share the executable's globals : the host hands it the engine, the component registry and the logger when it loads, and the context only holds pointers to the host's objects.

Build fingerprint. The library carries a string made of the OS, architecture, compiler, build type, and whether the physics are double precision and deterministic (SHARD_DOUBLE_PRECISION_PHYSICS, SHARD_DETERMINISTIC_PHYSICS). A library built another way than the executable is refused, with both strings in the message. Build plugins with the same CMake options as the engine they run in.

A plugin can also be compiled into the executable : declare it with SHARD_STATIC_PLUGIN(Class, "<manifest json>") (or PluginManager::AddStaticPlugin before startup) and give its manifest "linkage": "static". It goes through the same resolution, lifecycle and registration as a library. A static library may drop a translation unit nothing references, so reference the plugin explicitly if you declare it that way.

Libraries that predate this (they export InitializeSingletons and RegisterGameComponents) still load, as a code module, with a warning. They get no build check and cannot be reloaded.

docs.title: The C ABI and the SDK
docs.text: A plugin can be written against the Shard SDK (sdk/include/shard) instead of the engine's C++ headers. It links nothing of the engine and includes none of its headers. It loads in every engine with the same ABI major revision and a minor revision at least as recent as its own, whichever compiler built either side. A plugin built with MSVC loads in an engine built with MinGW GCC, and one built with Clang loads in an engine built with GCC. The CI checks both.

docs.title: Two layers, one door
docs.text:
The plugin and the engine are compiled separately, maybe by different compilers, so they cannot share C++ objects : a std::string or a class built by one compiler is not readable by the other. They talk through a narrow door instead, made only of plain C : integers, floats, pointers, and tables of functions. That door is the C ABI ("ABI" means the binary contract : which functions exist, in which order the fields of a struct are laid out, what each call expects).

Writing to that door by hand is tedious. Registering one component takes a struct describing each field, a table of callbacks, error codes to check after every call. So the SDK adds a second layer, written in C++, that does this for you :

  • The C ABI (shard/shard.h and the headers it includes) is plain C11. It is the contract between the plugin and the engine. The engine implements it.
  • The C++ SDK (shard/game.hpp and the shard/cpp/ headers) is header-only C++17 on top of the C ABI. It only wraps the C functions : s.Each(spin, ...) ends up calling the C function that walks a chunk of entities. It is compiled into your plugin, so it can use the standard library freely. Nothing of it crosses the door.

A rough picture :

your code  ->  C++ SDK (in your plugin)  ->  C ABI (the door)  ->  the engine
 Spinner        wraps, checks errors         plain C functions       does the work
C ABI alone C++ SDK on top Language C (or anything that can call C) C++17 Code to write long : structs, tables, error codes short : classes, lambdas, exceptions Mistakes yours to catch (an error code ignored is silent) the SDK checks, and turns a failure into an exception that is caught at the boundary Speed what you write the same, see below Needs the headers shard/*.h the same headers and shard/cpp/*.hpp

Both produce the same kind of plugin ("abi": "c1"), and the engine cannot tell them apart. You can even mix them in one plugin, for example the SDK for everything and a few direct C calls in a hot loop.

docs.title: Does the SDK make a plugin slower ?
docs.text:
Not by itself. The SDK is made of templates and small inline functions, which the compiler flattens : a loop written with s.Each compiles to the same loop as the one written in C. The part that does cost something is the same in both cases : each call across the door is a function call, and the engine hands out entities by chunk (a block of several hundred), so a system pays one call per chunk, not one per entity.

What can cost is C++ convenience used in the middle of a hot loop. These are things a C programmer would see as expensive, and the SDK makes them easy to write without noticing :

  • Anything that allocates (std::string, std::vector) inside the per-entity function.
  • A call that may throw an exception, made for every entity. The compiler has to keep the loop ready to unwind, which blocks some optimisations. SystemCtx::Emit was one of these : written inside a loop over 100 000 entities it made the system 1.4 to 1.7 times slower than the same system inside the engine. The SDK now keeps it out of line and takes a std::string_view (no temporary string), which brings it to about 1.1.
  • A call made once per entity that could be made once per frame (reading s.DeltaTime() inside the loop instead of before it).

The rule of thumb : in the function given to Each, do the arithmetic on the component, and call anything else only when something happens (an event, a destroy, a log line). Everything outside a system's loop (OnLoad, console commands, editor panels, one event per frame) is not measurable. Numbers, for a trivial system on 100 000 entities : same as the engine when the loop is clean, 1.1 times with an Emit that fires rarely. A sandboxed (WASM) plugin is a different case : the same loop runs about 20 times slower, which is the price of the isolation, see the sandbox.

If a profile ever shows the C++ layer in the way, the C ABI is always there : the headers are included anyway, so that one system can call the tables of shard_ecs.h and shard_systems.h directly (tests/plugin_fixtures/c_plugin/c_plugin.c does it for every interface) while the rest of the plugin stays in the SDK.

docs.title: The two levels of the C++ SDK
docs.text:
The C++ SDK itself has two levels. The gameplay level is how a game is written : classes that live on actors, like the engine's own scripts, in as many files as you want.

// health.hpp
#include <shard/game.hpp>

class Health : public Shard::Script {
public:
    SHARD_FIELD(float, maxHealth, Range(1.f, 1000.f)) = 100.f;      // a field : shown in the inspector, saved with the world
    SHARD_FIELD(float, current) = 100.f;

    void OnPlay() override { current = maxHealth; }
    void OnTick(float deltaTime) override { if (current <= 0.f) Owner().Destroy(); }
};

// health.cpp
#include "health.hpp"
SHARD_REGISTER_SCRIPT(Health)                           // registers the class

// module.cpp, once
SHARD_GAME_MODULE()

The registration level underneath is for a plugin that is not a game, or that fits in one file. It registers components, systems, variables and commands by hand in OnLoad :

#include <shard/cpp/plugin.hpp>

struct Spin { float speed = 1.f; float angle = 0.f; };
SHARD_COMPONENT(Spin, (speed)(angle))

class SpinPlugin : public Shard::Plugin {
public:
    void OnLoad(Shard::Context& ctx) override
    {
        auto spin = ctx.Components().Register<Spin>("Spin");
        ctx.Systems().Add("rotate", Shard::Phase::Update)
            .Writes(spin)
            .Run([spin](Shard::SystemCtx& s) {
                s.Each(spin, [&](Spin& c) { c.angle += c.speed * s.DeltaTime(); });
            });
        ctx.CVars().Float("scale", 1.f, "multiplies every speed");
    }
};
SHARD_C_PLUGIN(SpinPlugin)

You can mix them. A game can have scripts in some files, systems in others (SHARD_ON_LOAD, SHARD_DEFINE_COMPONENT), and a class derived from Shard::Plugin for variables, commands and hot reload. The tutorial builds one.

The manifest of such a plugin says "abi": "c1", and its entry point is shard_plugin_entry instead of shard_plugin_describe. shard_sdk_add_plugin (outside the repository) and shard_add_plugin(... ABI c1) (inside it) write both. The C ABI reference lists every function.

docs.title: Getting the SDK
docs.text:
The SDK is a folder : include/ (the C ABI and the C++ SDK), cmake/ (find_package(ShardSDK) and shard_sdk_add_plugin), bin/ShardPkg, templates/plugin/ and VERSION. Its version is the C ABI revision. To get it, run cmake --install build --component sdk --prefix <dir> on an engine build (it goes to <dir>/sdk), or build the ShardSDKArchive target, which writes build/shard-sdk-<version>.zip. The CI publishes that archive for each OS.

find_package(ShardSDK 1.0 REQUIRED)
shard_sdk_add_plugin(weather
    MANIFEST    shard-plugin.json      # the SDK adds "abi", "linkage" and "binaries"
    SOURCE_DIRS src                    # every .cpp under src/
    CONTENT_DIR content
    PACKAGE)                           # adds the target weather_package

SOURCES lists files one by one, SOURCE_DIRS takes every .cpp, .cc, .cxx and .c under a folder (CMake looks again when a file is added). PACKAGE adds a <target>_package target that packs the plugin with the SDK's ShardPkg into <build>/plugins/<id>.shardplugin. Without a MANIFEST, give ID and VERSION, and optionally KIND, MODULE_KIND, HOSTS, DEPENDS and AFFECTS_SIMULATION. The manifest is then written for you.

docs.title: What the C ABI offers
docs.text:
A plugin asks for interfaces by name and version : host->query_interface("shard.systems", 1, 0, &table). The C++ SDK does this for you.

Interface What it does shard.plugin 1.2 the plugin's id, version and folder. The host it runs in and its permissions (1.1). Random streams (1.2) shard.cvars 1.0 console and config variables shard.commands 1.1 console commands. Running a console line (1.1) shard.components 1.4 component types described field by field, each one an ECS component and an actor component. Blobs (1.1), text and asset fields (1.2), actor references and plugin-owned strings in scripts (1.3), on_added / on_removed / on_changed (1.4) shard.ecs 1.1 queries by chunk, component access and structural changes, from inside a system. Moving the actor behind an entity (1.1) shard.systems 1.0 systems in the scheduler's phases, with their reads, writes and order shard.events 1.1 events by name, carrying bytes. C++ code reaches the same channel. Describing a payload for the tools (1.1) shard.hooks 1.0 the engine's hooks, by name, cancellable shard.services 1.0 tables of functions that plugins offer each other, by name and version shard.extensions 1.0 asset validators, asset types and asset importers shard.content 1.0 module content : mod:// addresses, logical paths, reading files shard.state 1.0 what a plugin keeps across a hot reload, as JSON text shard.scripts 1.2 script types : classes of the plugin that live on actors. Physics contacts (1.1), edit mode and field changes (1.2) shard.actors 1.2 the actors of a world : pose, hierarchy, tags, creating and finding them, the engine's components as JSON. Stable ids, bounds, finding in a sphere or a box (1.2) shard.input 1.1 keyboard, mouse and gamepads. The events of the frame, clipboard, cursor shape, text input, capturing the input (1.1) shard.physics 1.1 velocities, forces, impulses, gravity and ray casts. Every hit of a ray, overlaps, sweeps, static colliders without an actor (1.1) shard.audio 1.0 the sound of an actor, one shot sounds shard.worlds 1.1 loading a world, spawning a prefab by name. The loaded worlds (1.1) shard.editor 1.2 panels, menu items, toolbar buttons, inspectors, viewport gizmos, the selection and notifications of the editor, with a wide set of widgets. A drawing canvas, undo entries, asset openers and templates (1.2). Only the editor offers it ; a sandboxed plugin needs the permission editor shard.jobs 1.0 the engine's worker threads : jobs, parallel loops, posting back to the main thread shard.time 1.0 frame, fixed step and simulation time, the time scale, a hash of the simulation state shard.assets 1.0 assets by path or id : listing, reading and writing files, the triangles of a mesh, the pixels of an image shard.reflect 1.0 the component and event types with their fields, and functions plugins register and call by name shard.net 1.0 UDP and TCP sockets, polled at the start of the frame (permission net) shard.render 1.0 meshes, textures, materials, objects, instance and sprite batches, a 2D overlay, the camera shard.debug 1.0 lines, shapes and texts shown for a duration shard.experimental.world_ecs 0.1 the engine's entities from the main thread, outside systems (experimental, see below)

The lifecycle callbacks are those of IPlugin, plus the frame, content and world callbacks of EnginePlugin and IModule, and on_tool_task of ToolPlugin.

The C ABI has no render pipelines or features of its own (a plugin draws objects, sprites and a 2D overlay into the engine's frame, see below), no ImGui itself (a plugin draws with the editor's widgets, see below), no physics joints or shapes beyond the body component's fields and the static colliders of shard.physics, and no audio mixing or effects. The engine components that have no interface of their own can still be read and changed as JSON through shard.actors. A plugin that needs more is written in C++ against the engine.

docs.title: Scripts, actors and input
docs.text:
A script type (shard.scripts) is a class of the plugin that lives on an actor. The plugin describes its size, its fields and its callbacks, and the engine registers it as an actor component named <plugin id>.<name>. It is built on the engine's own Script component, so :

  • the world ticks it in the same order as the engine's scripts (the order the components were added),
  • play mode starts and stops it,
  • the world file saves its fields and the inspector shows them,
  • a copy of the actor made for play mode builds a new object and copies the fields into it.

The object lives in storage held by the component, up to 16 KB. The plugin's own functions construct and destroy it in place and the engine never moves it, so it can have any member, including a std::vector. Fields are described like a component's, with ShardFieldDesc : numbers, booleans, vectors, quaternions, colours, text, assets and blobs, at their offsets in the object.

The callbacks are OnCreate, OnPlay, OnTick(dt), OnFixedTick(dt), OnLateTick(dt), OnStop, OnDestroyed, OnActivated, OnDeactivated, OnWorldLoaded and OnWorldUnloaded. They mean what they mean for the engine's scripts.

The scripts of a world run one after the other on the thread that ticks them, never two at once. This is why they can use shard.actors and shard.input, which a system cannot (systems run side by side). A script can destroy its own actor or add components in a callback : the world ticks the scripts it had when the tick began and skips the ones removed in the meantime.

shard.actors works with ShardActor handles, made of a generation and a slot. A destroyed actor fails with SHARD_E_STALE_HANDLE, and its handle never refers to another actor. It can :

  • read and set the pose, the name, the active state, the parent, the children and the tags,
  • create an actor, spawn one from the JSON a world file holds, find one by name or by tag, and destroy one,
  • add, test, remove, read and set the engine's components by the name their serialized form uses ("light", "model", "physics_body"), with their fields as JSON. Anything the editor shows can be reached this way.
  • read, set and erase one field of a component (shard.actors 1.1), by its name or a path into it ("materials/0", "shapes/0/params/radius", "shapes/-" to append). A field of the engine is set the way an edit in the inspector sets it, so a physics body keeps its velocity when its friction changes. The C++ SDK wraps these in typed handles (actor.Add<Shard::Model>().SetMesh(mesh), Shard::PhysicsBody, Shard::Light...).

Creating and searching work in the world of an actor that you pass in. A script passes its owner.

shard.input reads the engine's input manager, which is what replays record, so a script that reads its input here behaves the same in a replay. Key and button numbers are part of the ABI.

Random numbers (shard.plugin 1.2). rand(), std::random_device and std::uniform_*_distribution give other numbers from one run, platform or standard library to the next, so a replay that used them would drift. random_stream returns the state of a generator for a named stream, derived from the run's seed, the plugin's id and the name : the same name gives the same sequence when the run is replayed. The generator is PCG32, the engine's own Core::Random, and the SDK's Shard::Random runs it inside the plugin, so drawing a number is not a call into the engine and gives the same bits. Name a stream after what draws from it ("Spawner/" + Owner().Name()), not after the order scripts started in.

void RandomKicker::OnPlay() { m_Random = Shard::Random::Stream("RandomKicker/" + Owner().Name()); }
void RandomKicker::OnTick(float) { Owner().AddImpulse(m_Random.OnUnitSphere() * strength); }

Contacts (shard.scripts 1.1). A script with a physics body is told when it touches another body : on_contact_added, on_contact_persisted and on_contact_ended (OnContactAdded, OnContactPersisted, OnContactEnded in C++). Each gets a ShardContact : the other actor, a point of the contact, the normal and the penetration depth. The normal points from the script's actor toward the other one. The end of a contact has the other actor only. Both actors of a pair get the call, each with its own point of view.

Actor references and strings in scripts (shard.components 1.3). A script field of type SHARD_FIELD_ACTOR holds a ShardActor. The world file saves it as the path of the actor, "Level/Enemy" (root first, then the children's names). When the file is loaded, or a copy is made for play mode, the actor named by the path may not exist yet : the engine keeps the path, looks again before each callback, and fills the handle on the first call where the actor is there. An actor that is destroyed leaves an empty reference, never a dangling one. In C++ the field is a Shard::Actor (check it with if (target)). References are for scripts only, because a plain component block has no way to hold a path. They count against the same 8 text fields as strings.

A script can also list a string that the plugin owns, a std::string in C++. Such a field is flagged SHARD_FIELD_ACCESSOR, and gives text_get and text_set in the script's callbacks so that the engine reads and writes it through the plugin. The std::string itself never crosses the ABI, which is what keeps it safe between compilers : only the bytes do. Components still use Shard::Text.

Physics (shard.physics). Takes the handle of an actor with a physics_body component. It reads and sets the velocity and the angular velocity, adds forces, torques and impulses (at the centre or at a point of the world), reads the gravity that acts on the body and gives it a gravity of its own. A force lasts for the step it is added in, so a script that wants to push for longer adds it every fixed tick. Units are metres, kilograms, seconds and newtons.

raycast returns the first body on a ray : its actor, the point, the surface normal and the distance. layers limits it to static bodies, moving bodies or both, and ignore is an actor the ray goes through, which is usually the one firing it.

void Turret::OnFixedTick(float)
{
    auto hit = Shard::Physics::Raycast(Owner().WorldPosition(), Owner().Forward(), 50.f, Shard::Layers::All, Owner());
    if (hit) hit->actor.AddImpulse(Owner().Forward() * 5.f);
}

Audio (shard.audio). play, pause and set_volume act on the audio component of an actor. play_one_shot plays a clip of the project once, from a place in the world or flat, with no actor, and frees itself when it ends. A host with no sound device accepts every call and plays nothing.

Worlds and prefabs (shard.worlds). load_world asks for a world by its path in the project. The load is a request : it runs in the background and the world is swapped in at the start of a later frame, so the script that asked keeps running with everything it holds until then. is_loading and loaded_count tell where it is. spawn_prefab builds an actor from a JSON file of the plugin's content, by mod:// address, logical path (prefabs/crate.json) or bare name (crate), under a parent or at the root of the world. Before this, a plugin had to pass the actor's JSON itself.

Panels in the editor (shard.editor). ImGui has no stable ABI, so a plugin never calls it. It adds a panel, a window of the editor's Window menu, and draws its contents with the widgets ShardUiApi offers : text, buttons, checkboxes, sliders, drags, text boxes, colour pickers, combos, trees, progress bars and plots. The draw function runs every frame the window is open, on the editor's main thread, and only then may it use the widgets. Only the editor offers shard.editor. In the player, in a headless run and in the offline tools the interface is not found, the panel is not added, and the same plugin loads everywhere. A plugin whose hosts include engine is loaded by the editor like by the player, and editor alone limits it to the editor.

SHARD_EDITOR_PANEL(Spawner, "Enemy spawner", ui)
{
    static int count = 5;
    ui.SliderInt("Count", count, 1, 50);
    if (ui.Button("Spawn")) SpawnEnemies(count);
}

More of the editor (shard.editor 1.1, in the same header shard/cpp/editor.hpp). Everything a plugin adds goes with the plugin (disabled, reloaded : the editor calls OnEditorInit again, and the windows that were open are open again). Nothing is added outside the editor, and the same plugin runs everywhere.

SHARD_EDITOR_MENU_ITEM(BakeAll, "Tools/Bake/All levels") { BakeEverything(); }          // an item of the menu bar, nested menus with '/'
SHARD_EDITOR_TOOLBAR_BUTTON(Ping, "Ping") { Shard::Editor(Shard::detail::PluginHandle()).Notify("pinged"); }
SHARD_EDITOR_INSPECTOR(Health, "my.plugin.Health", ui, actor) { ui.SeparatorText("Debug"); ui.Text(actor.Name()); }   // below that component
SHARD_EDITOR_GIZMO(Range, gizmo, actor) { gizmo.Sphere(actor.WorldPosition(), 5.f); }       // in the viewport, for each selected actor
SHARD_ON_LOAD(Follow, ctx) { ctx.Editor().OnSelectionChanged([](const std::vector<Shard::Actor>& selected) { /* ... */ }); }

The widgets of Ui go from text, buttons and sliders to tabs, tables, menus, popups, groups, child regions and disabled sections ; Gizmo draws lines, points, circles, spheres, boxes, arrows and text in the world. Editor::SelectedActors() gives the selection, Notify shows a toast. A function a longer editor has and an older one lacks does nothing and returns false. A sandboxed plugin (tier 2) does all of this too, with "permissions": ["editor"].

A call into a script goes through the plugin like any other. The plugin is named as the one running, so a crash is blamed on it. An exception is caught, and an error returned counts as an error of the plugin : at the tenth, the engine fails the plugin, as it does for a system. When the plugin is disabled or unloaded, its scripts stop being called, so a world that still holds them never calls into a library that has left.

docs.title: Bigger systems (ABI 1.7)
docs.text:
ABI 1.7 adds what a particle system, AI and navigation, voxels, a runtime UI, animation, networking or a visual scripting editor are built from. None of them is in the engine ; each is a plugin made of these pieces, through the C++ headers shard/cpp/jobs.hpp, time.hpp, assets.hpp, reflect.hpp, net.hpp, render.hpp and debug.hpp (all included by shard/game.hpp).
