A plugin that makes... ...is built on particles SpriteBatch / InstanceBatch (one call per frame, a few thousand quads), Jobs::ParallelFor to update them, Script with kExecuteInEditMode to preview in the editor AI and navigation Assets::ReadMesh (the triangles to build a navigation mesh), Physics::Raycast*, Overlap* and Sweep* (visibility, steering), Collider (obstacles), Debug (paths, volumes), Scene::FindInSphere voxels Mesh made by a MeshBuilder (dynamic, updated when a chunk changes), Collider::Mesh or Collider::Boxes for the same chunk, Texture for an atlas, Jobs to mesh chunks off the main thread a runtime UI Overlay::Add and its Canvas (premultiplied-alpha triangles, scissor, textures) ; Input::Events, Modifiers, Clipboard, CursorShape, Capture to receive input and to keep it from the game animation a skinned Mesh (joints and weights) with RenderObject::SetBonePose (skinning is done on the CPU for now), Time::Now(), Actor::StableId to save a rig networking Net::OpenUdp / Connect / Listen, Time::Hash() to compare the simulation with a peer's, Time::Now().fixedStep as the tick number, Jobs::PostMain to hand a result back visual scripting Reflect::Types and Functions for the nodes, Reflect::AddFunction to add some, Commands::Execute, Ui canvas methods for the graph, Editor::PushUndo, Editor::AddAssetOpener and AddAssetTemplate for a graph asset 
// A static collider and a mesh for the same voxel chunk, built off the main thread
Shard::Jobs::Run([chunk] {
    Shard::MeshBuilder builder;
    chunk->Mesh(builder);                                   // quads for the visible faces
    Shard::Jobs::PostMain([chunk, builder = std::move(builder)]() mutable {
        chunk->mesh.Update(builder);                        // main thread : the GPU copy follows
        chunk->collider = Shard::Collider::Mesh(chunk->vertices.data(), chunk->vertexCount, chunk->indices.data(), chunk->indexCount, chunk->origin);
    });
});

What to know. Everything a plugin creates (meshes, textures, objects, batches, overlays, sockets, colliders, jobs) belongs to it and goes with it ; the handle classes of the C++ layer release theirs. Creating and updating a resource only records it (any thread, so a job can build a mesh) : the GPU copy is made by the thread that draws, a frame later. An object whose mesh was destroyed is not drawn. Limits of the first version : no texture arrays, a 2D clip mask is its bounding rectangle (no stencil), sprites and overlays are drawn on OpenGL and on Vulkan (on Vulkan an overlay packs its geometries again every frame), the debug shapes ignore the depth test, and a skinned mesh is skinned on the CPU. The sandbox does not offer these interfaces yet.

docs.title: Components across the ABI
docs.text:
A type that a plugin registers has two parts under one name (<plugin id>.<name>) :

  • an ECS component : a block of plain data on an entity, copied with memcpy and never constructed. Systems query it and write it.
  • an actor component : what a world file saves, the inspector shows and an actor carries. It is made of the fields the plugin described (floats, integers, booleans, vectors, quaternions, colours, and since ABI 1.3 text and assets).

When an actor has the component, its entity has the block with the same values. The actor component writes its values to the entity when it is loaded, edited, attached or activated, and reads them back when the world is saved or copied for play mode. What a system changed is therefore what gets saved. A deactivated component leaves the entity, so systems skip it. An entity that a plugin spawned itself has no actor and is not saved.

Field flags : SHARD_FIELD_RUNTIME shows the field read-only and does not save it, SHARD_FIELD_PRIVATE neither shows nor saves it. A component is at most 1024 bytes, aligned on at most 16, with at most 64 fields. Its ECS id is kept for the whole run : a plugin that is enabled again gets the same id back, as long as the size did not change (a new layout needs a restart).

Blobs (ABI 1.2) hold what does not fit in the block. A blob is bytes that the engine keeps outside the block, counted against the plugin's memory budget and released with the plugin. A field of type SHARD_FIELD_BLOB holds its handle. The block is still plain data, so copying a block shares the blob. The actor component is the exception : it owns the blobs of its blob fields, saves their bytes with the world (base64), gives a copy of the actor copies of them, and frees them when the component is removed.

Text and assets (ABI 1.3). A field of type SHARD_FIELD_STRING holds the handle of a blob whose bytes are UTF-8 text. The block stays plain data, the inspector shows a text box, and the world file saves a string. Ownership works as for blobs. string_set and string_get of shard.components 1.2 read and write it without touching the blob (Shard::Text in C++, with Get() and Set()). A component has at most 8 string fields, and a string field cannot be SHARD_FIELD_PRIVATE.

A field of type SHARD_FIELD_ASSET is an int32_t : the id of an asset of the project, 0 for none (Shard::AssetId in C++). The inspector shows an asset picker, and the world file saves the asset by its name in the project, like the engine's own components. Neither type can be used in a described event, because an event payload is copied as bytes.

docs.title: Moving actors
docs.text:
A system cannot write the engine's own pose component through the pointers a query returns. The actor's Transform drives shard.LocalTransform and would overwrite the change. Instead, a system calls set_local_transform of shard.ecs 1.1 (SystemCtx::SetLocalTransform(entity, Shard::Pose) in C++), after declaring shard.LocalTransform in its writes :

auto local = ctx.Components().Find<Shard::Pose>("shard.LocalTransform");
ctx.Systems().Add("drift", Shard::Phase::Update)
    .Writes(sign, local)
    .Run([sign](Shard::SystemCtx& s) {
        s.Each(sign, [&](Shard::Entity e, Sign& c) {
            Shard::Pose p;
            p.position.x = float(++c.uses);
            s.SetLocalTransform(e, p);
        });
    });

The pose is relative to the parent. It is recorded and applied when the phase ends, on the main thread, after the structural changes. The actor's Transform takes it, so children, physics and the renderer follow, and the entity's LocalTransform then holds it. Until the phase ends, systems that read shard.LocalTransform still see the old pose, whether the phase runs on one thread or many.

If several systems set the same entity in one phase, the one whose name sorts last wins. Only what changed is applied, so setting the same pose every frame costs nothing. A deactivated actor ignores the call, and an entity with no actor (one the plugin spawned itself) gets SHARD_E_NOT_FOUND.

docs.title: Systems and threads
docs.text:
A system declares what it reads and writes, and can reach only those types through shard.ecs (an exclusive system can reach any). The scheduler runs the systems of a phase in parallel when they do not conflict, and the result is the same with one thread or many. ShardHeadless --check-plugins checks this.

Every function of the ABI says which thread may call it : any, system (from a system, so possibly in parallel) or main (the main thread, outside systems). A main function called from a system returns SHARD_E_WRONG_THREAD. An event emitted from a system is queued and delivered on the main thread at the end of the frame, with the queues taken in the order of the systems' names, so the order does not depend on which system finished first.

A system that returns an error, or throws in C++, counts as an error of the plugin. At the tenth, the engine fails the plugin, as for a C++ system. Every call from the engine into a C plugin (lifecycle, systems, events, hooks, commands, validators, importers, asset loaders) names the plugin as the one running, so a crash is blamed on it and the next start offers safe mode without it.

docs.title: Described events
docs.text:
The payload of a named event is bytes, and the sender documents their layout. Since ABI 1.2 the sender can also describe it to the engine, with the same fields as a component (describe in shard.events 1.1, ctx.Events().Describe<T>() in C++, EventRegistrar::DescribeNamed for a C++ plugin). The console then uses the description :

  • event.list lists the described events and their fields,
  • event.watch <name> logs every event sent under that name with its values ({ ticks: 3, axis: (0, 1, 0) }),
  • event.unwatch <name> stops.

docs.title: Experimental interfaces
docs.text:
Things that may still change are offered as shard.experimental.* before they are frozen into the ABI. These interfaces come with no compatibility promise : the major is 0, query_interface returns one only for its exact minor, and it can change or disappear in any engine revision. A native plugin carrying a valid signature from a trusted publisher (a distributed plugin) is refused them. They are for development, and for trying what the next ABI revision should contain.

There is one today, shard.experimental.world_ecs. It gives the engine's registry on the main thread (Shard::experimental::World in C++). It is opened and closed within one callback, and its structural changes are applied when it closes.

docs.title: Versions and the rules of the headers
docs.text:
The ABI has a major and a minor revision (SHARD_ABI_MAJOR, SHARD_ABI_MINOR, also the SDK's version). A minor revision only adds : functions at the end of a table, fields at the end of a struct, new interfaces. A plugin built for 1.0 therefore loads in an engine at 1.1, while a plugin built for 1.1 is refused by an engine at 1.0 (built for the C ABI 1.1, this engine has 1.0). Each interface has its own version as well : a plugin that needs has_permission asks for shard.plugin 1.1.

The headers follow these rules :

  • plain C, with fixed-size types in structs,
  • every struct starts with uint32_t structSize and only grows at its end,
  • handles (index and generation) stand for host objects, never pointers,
  • no exception crosses the boundary.

A handle that outlived its object (a cvar of a disabled plugin, a ShardEcs kept after the system's run) fails with SHARD_E_STALE_HANDLE instead of reading freed memory.

The build fingerprint does not apply to a c1 plugin, since the ABI revision is the contract. The tier does not change either : a C plugin is a native tier 1 plugin, signed or allowed like the others, and nothing isolates it.

docs.title: Module content
docs.text:
A module's content folder is mounted in the virtual file system as mod://<id>/, and every file in it can be read from there :

auto text = ctx.Content().ReadText("mod://com.acme.weather/tables/rain.json");

An address can't leave its mount : .. and absolute paths are refused.

The same files form a second view, by logical path (materials/stone.mat), in layers : modules in load order. A later layer replaces an earlier one only for the paths it lists in content.overrides. Otherwise the earlier file is used and the clash is written to the log and shown in the Plugins panel (plugin.conflicts). Tables, translations and patches are merged on purpose and never clash.

Asset ids of module files come from AssetRegistrar::GuidOf : derived from <asset namespace>/<path> (case and separators don't matter), so they are the same on every machine and do not depend on when a file was first seen.

If a world holds a component of a type that is not registered (its plugin is not loaded), the component is kept as it was read and written back unchanged when the world is saved. Opening a world without the plugin loses nothing.

docs.title: Datapacks
docs.text:
A datapack has no code. It is a folder :

my_pack/
  shard-plugin.json            kind "module", moduleKind "datapack"
  content/
    worlds/arena.world         a whole world
    patches/sponza.patch       a patch of an existing world
    prefabs/*.json             an actor with its components and children
    tables/weapons.json        data tables
    lang/fr.json               translations
    components/health.json     a component made of fields
    materials/ textures/ models/ sounds/   assets

Everything is checked when the pack loads ; a pack with a file that doesn't have the right shape is Failed and the message names the file. --validate-plugin does the same without loading.

  • Tables (tables/<name>.json, an object) are merged key by key across layers, the later layer winning : ContentMounts::LoadTable("weapons").
  • Translations (lang/<code>.json) are flat ("ui.start": "...") or nested, merged the same way : Translate(key, language, fallback).
  • Patches change a world file as it is read, so the world on disk is untouched. A patch names the world by its file name (room.world) and lists operations. Actors are found by their names, separated by /. If one operation is wrong the whole patch is skipped, with the reason in the log.
{ "world": "sponza.world", "ops": [
    { "op": "addActor",        "parent": "Room/Table", "actor": { "name": "Lamp", "components": [] } },
    { "op": "removeActor",     "path": "Room/Chair" },
    { "op": "setComponent",    "path": "Room/Lamp", "type": "light", "fields": { "intensity": 3.0 } },
    { "op": "addComponent",    "path": "Room/Lamp", "component": { "type": "..." } },
    { "op": "removeComponent", "path": "Room/Lamp", "type": "light" },
    { "op": "setSettings",     "settings": { "ambient_color": [0.1, 0.1, 0.1] } } ] }
  • Declared components (components/<name>.json) describe fields (bool, int, float, string, vec3, color) with defaults. Each one becomes a real component type under its name : it can be added to an actor, is saved and loaded with the world, copied with the actor and edited in the inspector like a component written in C++, and code reads it with DeclaredFieldsComponent::Get/Set. A component has up to 64 fields and 1 KB of them, and the names type, active and tags are reserved. It has no behavior of its own : that comes from a code module.

example_project/plugins/example-pack is a small datapack.

docs.title: Trust levels
docs.text:
Level What How it runs 0 first-party code : the engine's modules, your game native, in the process, built with the engine 1 a third-party native plugin native, in the process. Has to be signed by a trusted publisher, or allowed by the project 2 a sandboxed plugin experimental : a WebAssembly module ("abi": "wasm1") compiled and run by Wasmtime. It sees only its own memory, its callbacks share a budget of time per frame (budgets.frameMs) and its memory a ceiling (budgets.memoryMB) ; a trap or an exhausted budget stops the plugin, not the engine. It needs no signature, and has no files, network, clock or randomness of the system. It is the plugin you write for the C ABI (or the C++ SDK, shard/game.hpp), compiled for wasm32 : every interface of the ABI except the editor's, hooks, services and extensions, with the permissions of its manifest deciding which it is offered (fs.read:content, input, physics, audio, worlds.load, actors.spawn). Build it with shard_sdk_add_plugin(... TARGET wasm) and a wasi-sdk 34 or later (SHARD_WASM_TOOLCHAIN) ; what differs from a native plugin is in shard/shard_wasm.h 3 a datapack no code, validated against the formats above

A native plugin can do anything the process can. The permissions list tells the user what the plugin means to do, but nothing holds it to that. Install native plugins only from publishers you trust. What Shard checks is who made the files, not what they do.

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
A plugin folder can carry a shard-signature.json : an Ed25519 signature, by a named publisher, over the plugin's id, its version and the digest of all its files (every file except the signature and the install marker, by relative path and SHA-256). Changing, adding or removing a file, or the id or version in the manifest, makes the signature invalid. A plugin with an invalid signature is always refused. A valid one is trusted if the publisher is in a trust file and its key was not revoked :

{ "publishers": { "acme": "<64 hexadecimal digits>" }, "revoked": [ "<a key>" ] }

plugin-trust.json next to the project is read by default (--trust-file adds more). plugin.trust <publisher> <key> adds a publisher and saves it there ; plugin.verify <id> says who signed a plugin.

Where a signature is required :

  • a plugin that was installed from a registry (plugin.install leaves .shard-install.json in its folder) must carry a valid signature of a trusted publisher to load ;
  • a native plugin ("tier": 1) that is not signed that way is refused, unless the project's plugin entry says "allowUnsigned": true or the run has --allow-unsigned-plugins ;
  • any other plugin loads unsigned : plugins you put in the folder yourself are yours.

docs.title: Packaging, signing and registries
docs.text:
ShardPkg is the publisher's tool :

ShardPkg keygen acme --out keys                  # keys/acme.key (keep it private) and keys/acme.pub
ShardPkg sign my_plugin --publisher acme --key keys/acme.key
ShardPkg pack my_plugin --out com.acme.weather-1.4.2.shardplugin
ShardPkg verify com.acme.weather-1.4.2.shardplugin --trust plugin-trust.json
ShardPkg index registry/index.json add registry/com.acme.weather-1.4.2.shardplugin --name "Acme"
ShardPkg fingerprint                             # the build fingerprint of this engine, what `cpp` plugins are checked against

Sign first, then pack, then index : signing writes shard-signature.json into the folder, and the archive is made of the folder as it is. Without --out, pack names the archive <id>-<version>.shardplugin. The archive holds the manifest, the libraries and the content, and nothing else : the import library a Windows build produces stays in the build folder.

ShardPkg is installed in the SDK (sdk/bin) (on Windows with MinGW it is linked statically, so it runs without the engine or a compiler runtime next to it), so a plugin built outside the engine's repository can pack and sign itself : shard_sdk_add_plugin(... PACKAGE) finds it there (SHARD_PKG_EXECUTABLE points CMake at another one). It works the same way for cpp and c1 plugins.

A registry is a folder (or a web server's folder) with an index.json and the archives it lists. The index gives each archive's file name, size and SHA-256, its publisher, the engine versions it works with and its dependencies. Serve it over plain http:// ; https:// is not supported, and nothing depends on it : the archive is checked against the hash in the index, and its files against the signature.

In the editor or any executable with a project :

Command plugin.search [text] what the registries offer plugin.install <id> [range] downloads the plugin and the dependencies the registries can satisfy, checks size, SHA-256, the archive's paths and the signature, and puts them in the project's plugins folder. They load on the next start. An older version is replaced only once the new one is complete plugin.installed, plugin.updates, plugin.update <id> what came from registries, and newer versions inside the same major plugin.uninstall <id> removes a plugin installed from a registry (not while it is loaded, and nothing that was not installed that way)

An archive is refused if an entry would leave the folder it is unpacked into (.., an absolute path, a drive, a backslash), if it expands by more than a thousand times, or past 512 MB per file or 2 GB in all.

docs.title: Determinism and multiplayer
docs.text:
A plugin whose manifest says simulation.affects: true changes what the simulation computes, so everyone who shares that simulation needs the same one :

  • Each plugin has a hash made of its id, its version and the bytes of its content folder (the code is identified by the version : the same source gives other machine code on every platform). plugin.hash prints the set of running plugins that affect the simulation and the hash of that set.
  • A replay records that set as plugin lines. ShardHeadless and the player refuse to play a replay when the plugins loaded now differ from the recorded ones, naming the difference. A replay with no plugin lines is not checked.
  • ShardHeadless --server --port <n> answers a handshake over TCP : the client says which plugins (id, version, content hash) it runs, and the server welcomes it or refuses it, naming the difference. The PlayerConnecting hook and the OnClientConnect of the server plugins are asked too, and may refuse the client. With --offer-datapacks, a client that only lacks datapacks is offered them (id, version, size, SHA-256) and can fetch each one, check it and unpack it before restarting : code is never offered or sent. PluginHandshakeServer/PluginHandshakeClient (engine/plugins/handshake.hpp) are the two halves for a game that hosts its own clients ; ShardHeadless --check-server host:port asks a server from the command line.
  • Plugins with affects: false (interface, audio, visuals) are left out of the set.

ShardHeadless --check-plugins runs the simulation in two processes, with one job thread and with several, and fails when the state differs : run it in CI for a project whose plugins affect the simulation.

A deterministic plugin follows the rules of Headless mode and determinism : random numbers from ctx.MakeRandomStream, time from the fixed step, nothing from rand() or the clock. The stream is derived from the plugin id and the stream name, so adding another plugin doesn't change the numbers a plugin draws. Systems run in registration order, which is plugin load order, which is deterministic.

docs.title: Hot reload
docs.text:
A library built with SHARD_PLUGIN can be rebuilt and reloaded while the editor runs : plugin.reload <id> or the Reload button of the Plugins panel. The editor allows it ; the player with --hot-reload-plugins ; a deterministic run never does.

Windows keeps a loaded library locked, so with hot reload on the manager loads a copy from the temp folder and leaves the original free to be rebuilt. A reload :

  1. asks the plugin to save its state (OnPrepareReload writes JSON, and returns false if it can't be reloaded) ;
  2. sets the loaded worlds aside, since their components have code in the library (refused if a world has unsaved changes ; the worlds are put back afterwards) ;
  3. stops the plugins that depend on it, unloads the library, loads the new file, runs OnLoad, OnInitialize and OnEnable ;
  4. calls OnRestore with the saved state, and starts the dependents again.

If the new library does not load, the plugin is Failed with the reason.

docs.title: Console commands
docs.text:
Command plugin.list the plugins, state, and cost per frame plugin.info <id> everything about one plugin : what it registered, errors, warnings plugin.enable <id>, plugin.disable <id>, plugin.reload <id> plugin.services, plugin.hooks, plugin.extensions [point] what plugins offer and attached plugin.content [id], plugin.conflicts the mounted files, and the clashes plugin.hash the simulation plugin set and its hash plugin.lock [verify\|write] check or rewrite plugins.lock plugin.validate <folder> check a plugin folder without loading it plugin.budgets time per frame and counted memory against each plugin's budget plugin.search, plugin.install, plugin.installed, plugin.updates, plugin.update, plugin.uninstall registries, see above plugin.trust <publisher> <key>, plugin.verify <id> trusted publishers and signatures event.list the named events that plugins described (ABI 1.2) and their fields event.watch <name>, event.unwatch <name> log every event sent under that name with its values, or stop asset.import <file> [folder], render.features what plugins brought to the asset and render systems

The editor's Plugins window (Window menu) shows the same list, with the problems found at startup and buttons for enable, disable and reload.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause build fingerprint mismatch a cpp plugin was built with another compiler, build type or physics option than the executable. A plugin built with the SDK ("abi": "c1") is not checked this way built for the C ABI 1.x, this engine has 1.y the plugin was built with an SDK more recent than the engine : update the engine, or build against an older SDK does not export the C ABI entry point the manifest says "abi": "c1" but the library has no shard_plugin_entry : build it with shard_sdk_add_plugin or end it with SHARD_C_PLUGIN 'abi' must be "cpp" or "c1" a typo in the manifest's abi field an interface call returns SHARD_E_UNSUPPORTED an experimental interface (shard.experimental.*) asked by a plugin that is signed by a trusted publisher, or an engine that does not have it needs engine ..., built for plugin API ... engine.versions or engine.api doesn't fit this engine needs the engine feature ... the engine was built without it (largeWorld needs SHARD_DOUBLE_PRECISION_PHYSICS) no binary for linux-x86_64 the manifest has no library for this platform a plugin and its dependents are Failed a callback threw or a dependency failed : plugin.info <id>, and the log lines tagged with the plugin id two plugins conflict conflicts in a manifest : the one that sorts last by id is left out, unless the project requires it a file from a module is not used another layer provides it and this one does not list it in content.overrides a datapack is Failed a file doesn't have the right shape : the message names it ; --validate-plugin shows all of them the replay is rejected at start the plugins loaded now differ from the recorded ones ; the message lists the difference plugins.lock warnings a plugin changed since the lock was written : plugin.lock write after checking why a plugin is missing after a crash safe mode left it out for one run ; --ignore-safe-mode loads it a plugin shows in Rejections as untrusted its signature is invalid, or it is native / installed and not signed by a trusted publisher : the message says which, and what to add plugin.install says the SHA-256 differs the archive on the server is not the one the index describes : nothing was installed plugin.install says the plugin is unsigned or untrusted add the publisher's key to plugin-trust.json (plugin.trust), or install with --allow-unsigned-plugins if you accept the risk --check-plugins fails a plugin that affects the simulation depends on the number of job threads : its systems write what others read without declaring it, or it uses a thread of its own plugin.reload refuses hot reload is off in this run, the plugin was not built with SHARD_PLUGIN, or a loaded world has unsaved changes

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text: Shard renders with OpenGL 4.6 (default) or Vulkan 1.3. Both backends use the same shaders and produce the same image. Select one with --api opengl|vulkan (player, editor, headless) or the "api" field of the project.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Nothing to install. The Vulkan headers, volk, vk-bootstrap, VMA, glslang and SPIRV-Reflect are submodules, and the Vulkan runtime comes with your GPU driver.

You only need the Vulkan SDK for:

  • the validation layers (SHARD_VULKAN_VALIDATION=1)
  • slangc, to compile Slang shaders
  • vulkaninfo and the other SDK tools

docs.title: Render graph
docs.text:
Each pass declares what it reads and writes (RenderPass::graphAccesses and its target). RenderGraph (in renderer/rhi/graph) uses that to work out:

  • the order of the passes
  • which passes can be skipped because nobody uses their output
  • the barriers needed between two uses of a resource
  • which transient targets can share memory

The graph is independent of the graphics API and has its own unit tests.

  • render.graph [file.dot] prints the current frame's graph, and can write it as a Graphviz file.
  • A pass that names the passes it runs after reads what they wrote. This is how ping-pong targets work.

docs.title: Shaders
docs.text:
Shaders are written in GLSL 4.3. For Vulkan, ShardShaderCompiler compiles them with glslang using the relaxed Vulkan rules:

  • loose uniforms are collected into one uniform block
  • resources are assigned a descriptor set by kind: 0 textures, 1 storage buffers, 2 storage images, 3 uniforms, 4 bindless textures
  • sampler2D(handle) reads from the bindless array

Some drivers allow only 32 samplers in a fragment shader. lit.frag uses 11 : the material's textures (or the G-buffer), the sky, the reflection probe, one array per kind of shadow map, and the emission map. The engine's other textures (AO, reflections, lightmap pages, GI probe atlases) are read through bindless handles. The layout is listed at the top of lit.frag.

SPIRV-Reflect runs on the output. A compiled program is saved as a .spvpack (SPIR-V plus reflection data), keyed on a hash of the sources, defines and compiler version, so a stale file is never loaded.

ShardShaderc <shader root> <output dir> [--define NAME[=VALUE]] [--only name] [--reflect] [--force] [-j n]

--define builds a permutation. At runtime Shader::GetVariant does the same, for example for the G-buffer and deferred variants of lit.frag.

docs.title: Slang
docs.text:
.slang files work on Vulkan only. They are compiled with slangc (from the Vulkan SDK, or the path in SHARD_SLANGC), with vertexMain, fragmentMain and computeMain as entry points.

Uniforms that the engine sets by name go in the constant buffer at [[vk::binding(0, 3)]]. Textures are Sampler2D. See shaders/examples/slang_tint.slang.

On Vulkan, Shader::Create(file, file) loads a Slang shader directly, and shaderc precompiles them (skipped when slangc isn't found). Materials can't use Slang shaders yet, and there is no Slang compute asset.

docs.title: Render pipelines
docs.text:
A render pipeline asset defines how a frame is built. They live in resources/engine_resources/pipelines/*.renderpipeline. Pick one with "renderPipeline" in the project, or switch at runtime with render.pipeline <name>.

Pipeline Description forward+ Default. Meshes are lit while drawn, using clustered lights, a depth prepass and MSAA. deferred Opaque and masked geometry is written to a G-buffer and lit in one fullscreen pass. Translucent geometry and the sky are still drawn forward.

To add one, implement RenderPipeline and register it with RenderPipelineRegistry.

The editor's view modes work with both pipelines. In deferred, the lighting pass draws the Normals, Depth, Unlit, GI, SSAO and Shadow Cascades views from the G-buffer. The G-buffer pass writes the UVs, Lightmap UVs and Wireframe colours in place of the albedo. The Shaded Wireframe lines come from one more sweep over the G-buffer's draws. To support the view modes in your own pipeline, set RenderPass::debugViewRole on its passes. A pipeline whose SupportsView returns false for a view falls back to forward+ while that view is on.

docs.title: Shadows
docs.text:
The shadow settings are in Project Settings > Rendering, in the Shadows, Directional Shadows, Spot Shadows and Point Shadows groups. They are saved in rendering.shadows in the project file and applied at once (the shadow maps are rebuilt when a resolution, the number of cascades, Double-sided Casters or Conservative Rasterization changes; everything else takes effect on the next frame).

The suns share 9 cascade map slots, and each takes one per cascade : with 3 cascades 3 suns cast shadows, with 4 or 5 only 2, with 6 only 1. The suns beyond that are unshadowed.

Resolutions are the side of a square map in texels. A sun has one map per cascade (three by default), so its memory is the number of cascades times the square of its resolution.

The maps of each kind of light are the layers of one texture array : one for the suns' cascades, one for the spot lights, one cube map array for the point lights. lit.frag reads each array through a single sampler, so the number of shadowed lights does not use up sampler units. The arrays are sized to the lights that have a shadow slot, and are rebuilt when one is added beyond their size.

Setting Key Default Enable Shadows enabled on Off, every light is unshadowed. Directional Resolution directionalResolution 2048 Side of each cascade's map. Distance directionalDistance 0 How far from the camera the sun's shadows reach, in world units. 0 follows the camera's far plane. Cascades cascadeSplits, cascadeColors 3 cascades (splits 0.27, 0.54; red, green, blue) Edited as a bar : drag a handle to move the split between two cascades, right-click it to merge them, Split / Remove add or drop one. cascadeSplits holds where each cascade but the last ends, as a fraction (0 to 1, ascending) of the range from the camera's near plane to Distance ; cascadeColors holds one [r, g, b] per cascade, shown in the Shadow Cascades debug view. 1 to 6 cascades. Stabilize Cascades stabilizeCascades on Snaps each cascade to its texels so shadows don't shimmer when the camera moves. Caster Range casterRange 500 How far from a cascade, towards the sun, casters are still drawn. A caster further than this casts no shadow on it. Double-sided Casters directionalDoubleSided on Draws both faces into the sun's maps. With it off, only the faces turned away from the sun are drawn, which lets light through the edges of single-surface roofs and walls. Conservative Rasterization directionalConservativeRaster on Draws every texel a caster touches, so a gap thinner than a texel (the joints of a model) doesn't let a line of light through. OpenGL with GL_NV_conservative_raster only. Normal Bias directionalNormalBias 2 Texels the lit point is moved along the normal before the lookup, more on a surface that grazes the light. Depth Bias directionalDepthBias 0.75 Constant depth offset, in texels. Slope Bias directionalSlopeBias 1 Scale of the receiver plane bias that follows the surface's slope across the filter. Filter Radius directionalFilterRadius 2 The filter takes (2 × radius + 1)² taps. 0 is a single hardware filtered tap. Filter Spread directionalFilterSpread 1 Distance between two taps, in texels. Spot Resolution spotResolution 1024 Side of a spot light's map. Depth Bias / Minimum Depth Bias spotDepthBias / spotMinDepthBias 0.0005 / 0.00005 Slope scaled bias and its floor, in depth units of the map. Filter Radius / Spread spotFilterRadius / spotFilterSpread 2 / 1 Same as the sun's filter. Point Resolution pointResolution 1024 Side of each of the six faces of a point light's cube map. Depth Bias pointDepthBias 0.15 In world units. Filter Samples / Radius pointFilterSamples / pointFilterRadius 20 / 0.05 Taps (1 to 20) spread on a disc of that radius, in world units at the surface. 1 is a hard edge.

docs.title: Ambient
docs.text: World Settings > Ambient sets ambient_color in the world file : an HDR [r, g, b] (a component can exceed 1) added to every surface, scaled by its albedo, on top of the lighting. Worlds saved with the older single number ambient_intensity load it as a grey. A material can override it with an ambientColor uniform ([r, g, b]).

docs.title: Reflection probes
docs.text:
A Reflection Probe (Add Component > Reflection Probe) is a box of the world whose surfaces reflect a picture of what surrounds its actor, instead of the sky : indoors, a glossy surface reflects the walls of the room, not a sky it cannot see. Without a probe the reflection is the world's skybox, filtered by roughness.

Bake path traces the whole sphere around the actor with the offline raytracer (so the picture holds the lights, the bounces and the sky as the world has them) and saves it as an equirectangular .hdr in the project's reflection_probes folder, referenced by the world file like the baked GI probes. The picture is then loaded as a skybox would be : a cubemap, and a prefiltered cubemap with one level per roughness. reflection.bake and reflection.status do the same from the console.

Field Default Meaning Half Extent 5, 3, 5 The box the probe covers, centered on the actor (it does not follow the actor's rotation or scale). Bake Resolution / Samples / Bounces 1024 / 256 / 4 Width in pixels of the picture (the height is half), samples per pixel, light bounces. Intensity 1 Multiplier on the light of the reflection. Blend Distance 1 Distance inside the edge of the box over which the reflection fades into the sky's. Box Projection on Corrects the lookup for the size of the box, so the reflection of a wall lands where the wall is. Turn it off for an open area.

Only a material with useEnvReflections reflects a probe. One probe is used at a time, the one nearest to the camera (the smaller box when the camera is inside several).

docs.title: Screen-space reflections
docs.text:
World Settings > Screen-Space Reflections (ssr in the world file, off by default) makes a shiny surface reflect what the screen shows where its mirror ray lands, in place of the reflection probe's or the sky's. What the screen does not show falls back to them : a ray that leaves the screen, goes behind an object or finds nothing weighs 0. Only a material with useEnvReflections takes it, like the probe and the sky. Same shaders on OpenGL and Vulkan.

It is a chain of compute passes, the SSRPass of the render graph (after the SSAO depth + normal prepass, which it reads, and before the lighting) :

  1. Hi-Z : a pyramid of the closest depth of the prepass.
  2. Colour : the previous frame's HDR picture and its mips (the blur of a rough reflection). The scene is lit after the chain, so the colour a reflection shows is the last frame's, looked up where the camera had it.
  3. Trace : the hierarchical march of every pixel's mirror ray through the Hi-Z, at 1, 1/2 or 1/4 of the screen, blended with the frame before's hit (reprojected, world space) when Temporal is on.
  4. Resolve : one entry per pixel (edge-aware upsample) : where the hit is in the previous picture, how wide the specular lobe is there, and a confidence.

The prepass has no materials, so the trace does not know the roughness : it is the mirror ray. lit.frag applies the roughness where it is known, by the level of the colour pyramid it reads (roughness^2 wide) and by fading the reflection out of the surfaces rougher than Max Roughness. This means a GGX importance sampled trace (and the noise, and the denoiser it needs) is not what this is, and that the cost does not depend on the roughness of the pixels.

Field Default Meaning Quality Medium A preset of Max Steps, Resolution and Temporal (Low 32 / 1/4, Medium 48 / 1/2, High 64 / 1/2, Ultra 96 / 1). Touching one of them makes it Custom. Max Steps / Resolution / Temporal 48 / Half / on maxSteps, resolutionDivisor (1, 2, 4), temporal. Temporal Blend 0.85 How much of the previous frame stays. Lowered by itself while the camera moves. Intensity 1 How much of the reflection replaces the probe / sky one where a ray hit. Max Distance 50 How far a ray travels, in world units. Thickness 0.3 How far behind a surface of the depth buffer a ray may pass and still hit it. Max Roughness 0.6 Beyond it the surface is left to the probes and the sky (the fade starts at 60% of it). Roughness Blur 1 Scales the blur of a rough reflection. Edge Fade 0.1 Fraction of the screen from its edges over which a reflection fades out.

Orthographic cameras and the studio views (material previews) have no SSR. The textures are the size of the viewport (Hi-Z, colour pyramid, result and the two histories : about 260 MB at 4K on Half, 65 MB at 1080p), and the SSR Hi-Z, SSR Colour, SSR Trace and SSR Resolve GPU scopes show in the profiler.

docs.title: Texture filtering
docs.text: Textures that have mips are sampled with anisotropic filtering, 16x by default (render.anisotropy, 1 to 16, capped by the GPU). It is read when a texture is loaded, so a texture already in memory keeps its level until it is loaded again.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• Passes are labelled for RenderDoc with DebugScope. When RenderDoc is attached, the engine uses its in-app API (render.renderdoc, render.capture).
  • render.dump <dir> saves every pass target as a PNG, along with the graph.
  • render.screenshot <file> saves the last frame: a .hdr holds the scene in linear light, before exposure and tonemapping; a .png holds the picture as shown.
  • SHARD_VULKAN_VALIDATION=1 turns on the validation layers.

docs.title: Comparing against the path tracer
docs.text:
The offline path tracer (raytrace.render) is the reference the real-time lighting aims for. To find out which approximation is wrong, both renderers split the light leaving a surface into four terms (rhi/lighting_terms.hpp, LIGHTING_TERM_* in light.glsl):

Term What it is Real time direct the lights, straight onto the surface, shadowed clustered lights, shadow maps indirect_diffuse everything else arriving through the diffuse lobe: sky, bounces, emissive surfaces, ambient floor GI probes, lightmaps, sky irradiance, SSAO indirect_specular everything else arriving through the specular lobe environment map, reflection probes, SSR emission the surface's own light, and the sky where no surface is seen emission, skybox
  • render.lighting_terms <terms> makes the main view draw only some terms (all, none, or names joined by +). While it is not all, SSR keeps the reflections of the last full frame, and the sky is drawn only with emission.
  • raytrace.render <file.hdr> <w> <h> <spp> <bounces> terms also writes <file>.<term>.hdr. Every contribution of a path is tagged by the first surface it leaves (its own emission, the lights sampled from it, or the lobe the path continues by), so the term images add up exactly to the picture.
  • render.camera <px> <py> <pz> <tx> <ty> <tz> [fov] draws the frames (and what raytrace.render traces) from another view: a position, the point it looks at, the vertical field of view. It leaves the simulation alone. render.camera off goes back to the active camera, and render.camera alone prints the view and the extent of the meshes.
  • python scripts/compare_reference.py --world sponza.world runs both from the world's views in scripts/reference_views.json (or its camera) and writes build/reference_compare/<world>/report.html. For each term, over all views and for each view, it gives the term's share of the light, the overall bias in stops, the error per area (too bright / too dark), and an error map. With --keep-reference, only the real-time side is rendered again.

A lightmapped surface takes the direct light of Static lights from its lightmap, so in real time that light counts as indirect_diffuse. Compare with Dynamic or Stationary lights to keep the terms apart.

docs.title: Editor on Vulkan
docs.text: ShardEditor --api vulkan draws Dear ImGui to the swapchain with imgui_impl_vulkan (see RendererAPI::PresentUI). Textures reach ImGui as descriptor sets created on the render thread.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
How to label worlds, actors and components with names, and find or filter them by those names, without adding a component or a script for it.

A tag is a dotted, hierarchical name : Enemy.Undead.Skeleton, Damage.Fire, Interaction.Door.Locked. Each dot goes one level down a tree, so a tag is also every one of its parents : something tagged Enemy.Undead.Skeleton answers yes to "is it an Enemy ?" and to "is it an Enemy.Undead ?".

Everything lives in engine/core/tags/ : Core::Tag (one name), Core::TagContainer (a set of them), Core::TagQuery (a condition over a set) and Core::TagRegistry (the tree of every tag the project knows), reached with Core::TagRegistry::Get().

docs.title: The tree
docs.text:
Tags are declared once, for the whole project, and form a tree :

Enemy
├── Enemy.Undead
│   ├── Enemy.Undead.Skeleton
│   └── Enemy.Undead.Ghost
└── Enemy.Boss
Damage
├── Damage.Fire
└── Damage.Ice
Interaction
└── Interaction.Door
    └── Interaction.Door.Locked

Declaring Enemy.Undead.Skeleton declares Enemy.Undead and Enemy with it. A tag can come from three places, merged into the same tree when the project opens :

Source Where Typically Project "tags" in the project file, edited in Project settings > Tags the game's own tags Plugin "tags" in the plugin's manifest the tags a plugin's components look for Code SH_DECLARE_TAG(variable, "Name") in a .cpp tags a C++ system depends on, so it cannot be deleted from the editor 
"tags": {
    "Enemy.Undead.Skeleton": { "comment": "Breaks into bones, immune to poison" },
    "Enemy.Boss": {},
    "Damage.Fire": {},
    "Interaction.Door.Locked": {}
}

A name is made of segments of A-Z a-z 0-9 _ separated by single dots, and is case sensitive (Enemy and enemy are two tags). A tree is at most 8 levels deep.

The tree is built again when a source changes : when the project is loaded or its tags are edited, and when a plugin is loaded or unloaded. TagRegistry::Get().GetRoots(), GetInfo(tag) (name, parent, children, who declares it, comment) and CollectDescendants(tag, out) walk it.

docs.title: One tag
docs.text:
Core::Tag is a StringId (see engine/core/containers/string_id.hpp) that the registry knows : copying and comparing it costs one integer, and the text is kept for logs and the editor.

using namespace Shard::Engine::Core;

Tag skeleton = Tag::Request("Enemy.Undead.Skeleton");   // looked up in the registry
Tag parent   = skeleton.GetParent();                      // Enemy.Undead
bool under   = skeleton.IsChildOf(Tag::Request("Enemy")); // true
std::string text = skeleton.ToString();                   // "Enemy.Undead.Skeleton"

Tag::Request of a name the registry does not know returns the empty tag (IsValid() false) and logs a warning once per name : a typo does not silently create a tag nobody else uses. What a file holds is read with TagRegistry::Get().Resolve(name) instead, which keeps an unknown name (see Renaming and deleting).

For tags a C++ system tests every frame, declare them once and use the variable :

// door_system.cpp
SH_DECLARE_TAG(TagDoorLocked, "Interaction.Door.Locked");

if (actor->GetTags().HasTag(TagDoorLocked)) ...

The variable is filled before any world loads, so it can be used from OnCreate on.

docs.title: Who carries tags
Testing a set
docs.text:
A TagContainer holds the tags it was given (its explicit tags) and answers questions with their parents included :

Call True when the container has... {Enemy.Undead.Skeleton} with Enemy HasTag(t) t, or a child of t true HasTagExact(t) t itself false HasAny(other) at least one tag of other (with HasTag) HasAll(other) every tag of other (with HasTag) HasAnyExact / HasAllExact the same, with HasTagExact

The matching only goes one way : a container holding Enemy does not have Enemy.Undead.Skeleton. Tag things with the most precise name, and test with the most general one that the logic needs.

TagContainer& tags = actor->GetTags();

tags.Add(Tag::Request("Status.Burning"));
tags.Remove(Tag::Request("Status.Frozen"));

if (tags.HasTag(Tag::Request("Enemy")) && !tags.HasTag(Tag::Request("Enemy.Boss")))
    ApplyKnockback(actor);

Add of a tag the container already has does nothing ; Remove only removes an explicit tag (removing Enemy from {Enemy.Undead} does nothing, remove Enemy.Undead). RemoveWithChildren(t) removes t and every explicit tag under it.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
When a condition is more than one test, write it as a TagQuery : it can be built once, stored in a component field, edited in the editor, and evaluated against any container.

TagQuery hostile = TagQuery::All({"Enemy"})
                       .And(TagQuery::None({"Enemy.Boss", "Status.Dead"}));

if (hostile.Matches(actor->GetTags())) ...

The same query as text, the form it is saved and typed in :

Enemy & !(Enemy.Boss | Status.Dead)

& is and, | is or (looser than &), ! is not, parentheses group, and a bare name means HasTag. Write =Enemy for HasTagExact, and () for "nothing". TagQuery::Parse(text) returns an empty query (that matches everything) and logs the error when the text is not valid ; TagQuery::TryParse(text, query, &error) reports it instead. ToString() gives the text back.

A name the registry does not know, in the text or in All/Any/None, is kept and reported : that term matches nothing, it does not disappear and widen the query.

A reflected field of type TagQuery (or Tag, or TagContainer) is saved by name and has its own widget in the editor's inspector, so a designer can say which actors a trigger reacts to without code (run scripts/regen_reflection.sh after adding one, like any reflected field) :

class DamageZone : public Script {
    FIELD(Editable, tooltip=Which actors the zone hurts)
    TagQuery affects = TagQuery::Parse("Enemy | Player");

    FIELD(Editable)
    Tag damageType;
    ...
};

docs.title: Finding tagged things in a world
docs.text:
Each world keeps an index from tag to actors (and to components), updated when a tag is added or removed and when an actor joins or leaves the world, so a lookup does not walk every actor :

auto* world = actor->world;

std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Actor>> skeletons = world->FindActorsWithTag(Tag::Request("Enemy.Undead"));
std::shared_ptr<Actor> player = world->FindFirstActorWithTag(Tag::Request("Player"));
std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Actor>> targets = world->FindActors(TagQuery::Parse("Enemy & !Status.Dead"));
Call Cost FindActorsWithTag(t) the number of actors under t FindFirstActorWithTag(t) the same : the first of them FindActors(query) the actors under the query's required tag (a bare name, or a bare name in its top-level &), then the query tested on each. A query without one (A \| B, !A) tests every actor of the world FindComponentsWithTag(t) / FindComponentsWithTag<T>(t) the number of components under t

QuerySphere and QueryAABB add a position to it, so "the enemies within 10 m" is one call instead of a query and a loop :

std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Actor>> results;
world->QuerySphere(center, 10.0, TagQuery::Parse("Enemy"), results);
world->QueryAABB(Core::AABB(min, max), TagQuery::Parse("Pickup"), results);

They test the position of the actors FindActors finds (Transform::GetWorldCoords, in double) : the tags narrow the search first, they are not a spatial index.

The results are in the order of the actors' ids, so a deterministic run (see Headless & determinism) finds them in the same order every time. Deactivated actors (and components) are left out ; pass includeInactive = true to keep them.

docs.title: Reacting to changes
docs.text:
Changing tags in a loaded world emits a TagsChangedEvent to the scope of what changed, see Event system :

Tags of Scope Subscribe with an actor the actor subscribeToActor<TagsChangedEvent>(actor->GetID(), ...) a component the component, by its id in the world subscribeToComponent<TagsChangedEvent>(actor->GetComponentIDInWorld(component->GetLocalId()), ...) a world the world, by its asset id subscribeToWorld<TagsChangedEvent>(world->ResolveAssetID(), ...) 
events->subscribeToActor<Events::TagsChangedEvent>(actorID, [](const Events::TagsChangedEvent& e) {
    if (e.added.HasTag(TagBurning))
        StartFireParticles();
});

added and removed are the explicit tags that changed, in one event per Add, Remove, RemoveWithChildren, Clear or assignment (actor->GetTags() = other). Loading a world does not emit them. An actor's tags are read before its components, so a script's OnCreate already sees them ; a component's own tags come after it is created : read those in OnWorldLoaded or OnPlay.

docs.title: Renaming and deleting
docs.text:
Renaming a tag in Project settings > Tags renames it and all of its children, and adds a redirect per renamed name so worlds saved with the old name still load :

"tagRedirects": { "Enemy.Undead.Skelly": "Enemy.Undead.Skeleton" }

The open world is renamed at once (its actors, components, reflected tag fields and its own tags : Worlds::RemapTags) and marked as changed ; the other worlds take the new names through the redirects when they are loaded, and keep them once saved. The redirects are listed under the tree, where one can be removed.

The magnifier of a tag lists what uses it (or a tag under it) in the worlds of the project, and so does deleting one, before it is confirmed. The open world is searched as it is (exactly, field types included) ; the other worlds are read from their files, where any string of a component that reads as a query naming the tag is listed, even when it is not a tag field. A tag declared from code or by a plugin (or with such a tag under it) can be neither renamed nor deleted from the editor.

Loading a tag the project does not know (the plugin that declared it is not loaded, the redirect was removed, the tag was deleted) keeps it as it was read and writes it back on save, like unknown components, and logs a warning once. It matches only itself, and the editor shows it in orange.

docs.title: In the editor
docs.text:
• Properties : the actor's tags under its name, and a tags row at the top of each component. Click a tag to remove it, + to pick one in the tree (with a search box). Both edits can be undone.
  • World Settings > General : the world's own tags.
  • Reflected fields : a Tag is a button that opens the tree, a TagContainer the same chips as above, and a TagQuery a text field checked as it is typed (a red frame and the reason in its tooltip while it is not valid). It is applied when the field is left ; its + adds a tag as one more & term.
  • Project settings > Tags : the tree, who declares each tag, the comments (editable for the project's own), and add, rename, delete and find references. Saved with the project file, like the other settings.

docs.title: Rules to know
docs.text:
• Tags are labels, not state. A tag says what something is or is in (Enemy, Status.Burning). A value that changes every frame or carries a number belongs in a component field.
  • Not thread-safe to change. Add and remove tags from the main thread, outside parallel systems. Reading a container from a parallel system is fine as long as nothing changes it during the phase.
  • Tags are not collision layers. What collides with what stays in the physics settings ; a tag on a body only says what it is when a script reads it in OnContactAdded.
  • Keep the tree shallow and general. Enemy.Undead.Skeleton and Faction.Necromancer as two tags rather than Enemy.Undead.Skeleton.Necromancer : a tag answers one question.
  • Declare tags where they belong : the project, a plugin's manifest, or SH_DECLARE_TAG. The tree changes on the main thread only (a project edit, a plugin loaded or unloaded), never from a parallel system.

See also : Event system, Plugins for declaring tags in a manifest.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
How the engine measures time, and how a script should use it so a game behaves the same at 30 and at 300 FPS.

Everything lives in Time::TimeManager (engine/world/time_manager.hpp), reached with Core::GetEngine().GetTimeManager(). The engine ticks it once at the start of every frame.

docs.title: Two clocks
docs.text:
A frame runs with two kinds of time step :

Step Length Used by Variable (GetDeltaTime()) what the previous frame took, in seconds Update phase : scripts' OnTick, animation, audio Fixed (GetFixedDeltaTime()) constant, physics.fixedTimeStep in the project settings (1/60 s by default) Fixed phase : scripts' OnFixedTick, physics and gameplay that must not depend on the frame rate

The frame goes through the scheduler phases Input → PreSim → Fixed × N → PostPhysics → Update → Late → Extract. Fixed runs N times, N being the number of whole fixed steps owed this frame ; every other phase runs once.

docs.title: The accumulator
docs.text:
Real time is banked into an accumulator, and paid out as whole fixed steps :

accumulator += min(deltaTime * timeSpeed, maxAccumulatedTime)
steps       = floor(accumulator / fixedDeltaTime)     // ConsumeFixedSteps()
accumulator -= steps * fixedDeltaTime

So at 120 FPS about every other frame runs no step, at 30 FPS every frame runs two, and the simulation covers the same game time either way.

maxAccumulatedTime (physics.maxAccumulatedTime, 0.25 s by default) caps what one frame can bank. A frame that stalls (a breakpoint, a world load, a window drag) is clamped instead of owed in full, otherwise the next frame would have to run so many steps that it stalls too, and so on : the spiral of death. The price is that the game slows down instead of catching up.

The accumulator is emptied while the editor is not in play mode, so pressing Play does not replay a burst of steps.

docs.title: Smoothing the render
docs.text: What is left in the accumulator is how far the frame sits between two simulated states. GetFixedStepAlpha() gives it in [0, 1) ; the renderer uses it to interpolate transforms, so motion stays smooth when the render rate is not a multiple of the simulation rate.

docs.title: Script ticks
docs.text: Callback Phase Runs Step OnFixedTick() Fixed, right before the physics step 0..N times per frame GetFixedDeltaTime() OnTick() Update once per frame GetDeltaTime() OnLateTick() Late, after the physics results are back once per frame GetDeltaTime()

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text:
• Moving something in OnTick : multiply by GetDeltaTime().
  • Anything that must be reproducible (forces, timers that decide gameplay) : do it in the Fixed phase and use GetFixedDeltaTime().
  • Never accumulate GetDeltaTime() into a timer that decides gameplay : it differs from machine to machine.
void Character::OnTick(float deltaTime)      // the SDK passes the step ; engine C++ asks the time manager for GetDeltaTime()
{
    position += velocity * deltaTime;
}

docs.title: Time scale
docs.text:
SetTimeSpeed(x) scales how fast game time is banked : 0.5 is slow motion (half as many fixed steps per second), 0 freezes the simulation, 2 doubles it. In the console :

timescale          # prints the current value
timescale 0.25     # between 0 and 100

Note

The scale changes the number of fixed steps, not their length : physics stays stable in slow motion. It does not scale GetDeltaTime(), so variable-step code (OnTick) keeps running in real time. A script that should follow the scale multiplies by GetTimeSpeed() itself.

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text: Script callbacks run on the main thread, inside the frame. Never block in one (std::this_thread::sleep_for, PreciseSleep, future.wait()) : the whole game, the renderer included, stops until it returns. "Waiting" in a script means remembering that something is pending and checking again next tick.

docs.title: Wait for a duration
docs.text:
Keep a countdown in the script and decrement it each tick. For anything that decides gameplay, count in the Fixed phase so the delay lasts the same number of simulation steps on every machine :

void Door::OnFixedTick()
{
    if (m_CloseDelay <= 0.0f)
        return;

    m_CloseDelay -= Core::GetEngine().GetTimeManager()->GetFixedDeltaTime();
    if (m_CloseDelay <= 0.0f)
        Close();
}

void Door::OnOpened() { m_CloseDelay = 3.0f; }   // close 3 s of game time later

Counting in OnFixedTick also follows timescale (slow motion makes the delay longer, a freeze pauses it). A purely cosmetic delay can count GetDeltaTime() in OnTick instead, which stays in real time.

docs.title: Wait for a condition
docs.text:
Same idea, with a state instead of a number : test it each tick and act when it becomes true.

void Loader::OnTick()
{
    if (m_State == State::WaitingForWorld && world->IsLoaded())
    {
        m_State = State::Ready;
        Begin();
    }
}

When a script has several steps in sequence (wait, then do A, wait, then do B), write them as an enum class state plus a timer. There are no coroutines : a callback always returns.

docs.title: Wait for a point in the frame
docs.text: To act "after the physics", use OnLateTick rather than a flag checked next frame. To act on the next frame, set a boolean and test it at the top of OnTick.

docs.title: Running async code
docs.text: For work that is too long for a frame (decoding, a path search, building a mesh, reading a file), move it off the main thread and collect the result in a later tick. Two tools exist.

docs.title: Job system
docs.text:
Core::GetEngine().GetJobSystem() is a work-stealing pool. Submit a closure into a JobGroup, keep the group, and poll IsDone() each tick instead of calling Wait :

void Terrain::OnPlay()
{
    m_Job = std::make_unique<Core::JobGroup>();
    Core::GetEngine().GetJobSystem()->Submit(*m_Job, [this] {
        m_Heights = ComputeHeights(m_Seed);          // pure computation, no engine access
    });
}

void Terrain::OnTick()
{
    if (m_Job && m_Job->IsDone())                    // the result is ready : use it here, on the main thread
    {
        m_Job.reset();
        BuildMesh(m_Heights);
    }
}

JobSystem::Wait(group) blocks until the group is done. It is meant for code that has to join its own jobs inside one call (a parallel loop), not for "wait until the job finishes" across frames : in a script callback that is the same stall as a sleep. Do not destroy a JobGroup (or whatever the closure captures by reference) while jobs are still running ; if the script can be removed meanwhile, stop or finish the jobs in OnStop / the destructor.

docs.title: File IO
docs.text:
Platform::AsyncIO::ReadFile / WriteFile return a std::future<IOResult>. Poll it with a zero timeout :

if (m_Read.valid() && m_Read.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds(0)) == std::future_status::ready)
{
    IOResult result = m_Read.get();
    if (result.ok)
        Parse(result.data);
}

docs.title: Rules for async code
docs.text:
• Compute off-thread, apply on the main thread. A job must not touch the world, components, the renderer or the physics : none of them is thread-safe. Let the job fill data that only it owns, and apply it from OnTick once it is done.
  • A job must not throw, and must not block on something only another job will provide.
  • Capture by value what the job needs. A raw this is only safe if the script outlives the job.
  • The result arrives a frame or more later : the script has to cope with "not ready yet" (a flag, a state, IsDone()).
  • Async work does not follow the time scale or the fixed step. If the outcome must be reproducible (replays, deterministic runs), do not let gameplay depend on which frame a job finishes : wait for it, or apply it at a fixed point.

docs.title: Wall-clock time
docs.text:
Call Returns CurrentAppTime() time since the engine started, as a TimeStamp (monotonic steady_clock) CurrentGlobalTime() the local date and time of day (through the platform layer), days being the day of the year

TimeStamp splits a duration into days / hours / minutes / seconds / milliseconds / nanoseconds. Normalize() carries overflows up (1500 ms becomes 1 s 500 ms) and AsString() prints it as 0d 00h:01m:05s:250ms:000000ns.

docs.title: Deterministic runs
docs.text:
With EngineCreationSettings::deterministic (always in ShardHeadless, and with --record / --replay), the clock is not read : every frame lasts exactly one fixed step, so exactly one step is run per frame, whatever the machine is doing. See Headless mode and determinism.

To get the same without a full deterministic run (a benchmark, a test), set the time.frame_dt variable to a length in seconds : every frame then lasts that long. 0 (the default) is real time.

docs.title: Settings reference
docs.text: Setting Where Default Effect physics.fixedTimeStep project settings 1/60 length of a fixed step physics.maxAccumulatedTime project settings 0.25 most real time one frame may bank time.frame_dt variable 0 force the length of every frame timescale console command 1 speed of the simulation engine.maxFPS variable 0 frame rate cap (0 : none)

docs.title: Editor
docs.text:
ShardEditor (src/apps/editor) is the tool you build a game in : it opens a project, lets you edit its worlds, assets and settings, and runs the game inside its viewport so you can test a change without leaving it.

It is the same engine as the player, with an ImGui interface drawn on top of the Vulkan backend. The game module (the shared library holding your scripts and components) is loaded into it with --game, so the editor knows your reflected types and can show them in the properties panel.

docs.title: Role
docs.text: The editor... ...does not edits worlds, actors, components and assets ship with your game : players get ShardGame runs the game in play mode, inside the viewport write replays or benchmarks : that is the player's job saves the project and its worlds run without a window : use ShardHeadless

docs.title: Launching
docs.text:
ShardEditor --game plugins/game/bin/linux-x86_64/libGameModule.so --project example_project.json

--project is required : with none, the editor prints No project specified, aborting... and stops. --game is the game module to load (GameModule.dll on Windows).

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Option --project <file> project to open (required) --game <module> game module to load --width <n> --height <n> initial window size --fullscreen starts fullscreen --vsync <0\|1> vertical sync --api <opengl\|vulkan\|dx11\|dx12> graphics API --gravity <x> <y> <z> overrides the world's gravity --debug <log\|info\|warning\|error\|fatal> lowest log level printed (default log) --script <file> runs console commands at given frames, one <frame> <command> per line --frames <n> runs n frames, then closes without waiting for Enter : a non-interactive run, for smoke tests +name=value or +name value sets a console variable before the engine starts (+engine.maxFPS=60)

Without --frames, the editor waits for Enter before closing its console window.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
Every panel is toggled from the Window menu.

Panel What it does Viewport the scene, with the gizmos, the scene camera, the view modes and the visibility toggles. Also shows the statistics overlay and the offline raytrace controls World Tree the actors of the loaded worlds, as a tree with folders. Select (several at once), rename, group, drag to reparent, copy / paste Properties the reflected fields of the selected actors and their components. An edit is one undo step World Settings settings of the loaded world Asset Browser the project's assets : import, create, rename, reveal in the file explorer, drag into the viewport or the tree Console runs console commands and variables (timescale 0.5), and shows the log Profiler the time of the last frames by category, CPU and GPU Project Settings physics step, rendering and other project-wide values Editor Preferences how the editor itself behaves, stored per user and not in the project

Double-clicking an asset opens its own editor when there is one (the material editor, for example).

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
• Undo / Redo : every change goes through the command stack (Ctrl+W / Ctrl+Y), so a drag in the viewport or an edit in the properties panel can be taken back.
  • Tools : Move, Rotate and Scale gizmos ; F focuses the selection, End snaps it to the floor.
  • Selection : Ctrl+A selects all, Esc deselects, and the Select menu inverts the selection or selects the children.
  • Clipboard : Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+D duplicates, F2 renames, Ctrl+G groups, Del deletes.
  • Save : Ctrl+S saves the world.

docs.title: Play mode
docs.text:
Tools → Play Mode starts the game inside the viewport : scripts get OnPlay, then their ticks (see Time), and OnStop when you stop. Pressing Play first saves the first loaded world to its file ; stopping reloads it from there. What a script moves or destroys while playing is therefore thrown away, and the world comes back as it was when you pressed Play. F1 stops the play mode (the only editor shortcut that works while playing).

The accumulator is emptied while not in play mode, so pressing Play does not replay a burst of fixed steps.

docs.title: Exit
docs.text: The editor shuts the interface down, destroys the engine, then exits with code 0.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
ShardGame (src/apps/player) is the executable a game ships with. It loads a project and a game module, starts the first world in play mode and runs it with a window, the renderer and the audio. It has no editing interface : that is the editor.

It is also the tool for everything that needs the real game on a real GPU : smoke tests, benchmarks, screenshots, and recording sessions for replays.

Note

The CMake target is ShardGame (the source folder is src/apps/player). It is built as a Windows GUI application (WIN32_EXECUTABLE), so on Windows it has no console of its own : run it from a terminal to see the output.

docs.title: Launching
docs.text:
ShardGame --game plugins/game/bin/linux-x86_64/libGameModule.so --project example_project.json

--project is required. If no world can be loaded (a bad path, a broken file), the player stops with No world was loaded, aborting....

docs.title: Window and rendering
docs.text: Option --project <file> project to run (required) --game <module> game module to load --world <path> world to start with (default : the project's first world) --width <n> --height <n> window size --fullscreen starts fullscreen --vsync <0\|1> vertical sync --api <opengl\|vulkan\|dx11\|dx12> graphics API --gravity <x> <y> <z> overrides the world's gravity --debug <log\|info\|warning\|error\|fatal> lowest log level printed (default log) --view-mode <mode> debug view of the scene, as in the editor's viewport : lit, unlit, wireframe, shaded-wireframe, normals, depth, uvs, gi, ssao, lightmap-uvs, shadow-cascades +name=value or +name value sets a console variable before the engine starts (+engine.maxFPS=60) --script <file> runs console commands at given frames, one <frame> <command> per line

docs.title: Non-interactive runs
docs.text:
Option --frames <n> renders n frames, then shuts down. Nothing waits for Enter, the project is not written to (read-only) and the exit code tells whether it went well. This is what the CI smoke test uses (scripts/smoke_test.sh) --screenshot <file.png> writes the last rendered frame (the viewport, before presentation) to a PNG --bench with --frames, prints the average, median, p99 and worst frame time, the time per category, the render thread stats, the scene size and the RAM / VRAM in use, as [BENCH] lines --bench-warmup <n> frames left out of the benchmark at the start, for shader compiles and streaming (default 120) 
ShardGame --game plugins/game/bin/linux-x86_64/libGameModule.so --project example_project.json --frames 600 --bench --screenshot out.png

docs.title: Record and replay
docs.text:
Option --record <file> records the session's inputs, and the state of the simulation every --check-every frames, to a replay file --replay <file> plays a replay back : the keyboard is ignored, the file's inputs are fed to the game and its state checks are verified --seed <n> seed the random streams derive from (default : the replay's, otherwise 1) --check-every <n> frames between two state checks (default 60)

Recording or replaying makes the run deterministic : every frame lasts exactly one fixed step, and the project is left as it was found. A replay recorded with a different fixed step than the project's is refused. Playing a replay without --frames runs for as long as the replay does.

docs.title: Exit
docs.text:
Without --frames, the player prints Shard Engine has finished. Press Enter to exit... and waits, so the output stays readable when it was started by double-click.

Code Meaning 0 success (and the replay matched, if there was one) 1 a replay could not be saved, or the engine failed to start 2 the replay diverged : the simulation state differs from the recorded one

With --frames, a crash at startup exits with 1 right away instead of waiting for Enter.

docs.title: Main loop
docs.text: Each iteration of the loop calls Engine::Run() once : the scheduler goes through its phases (Input → PreSim → Fixed × N → PostPhysics → Update → Late → Extract, see Time), then the frame is presented. In a replay, the file's events are posted to the window before the frame and the state is checked after it.

docs.title: Write a game with the SDK
docs.text: This tutorial builds a game as a plugin, using only the Shard SDK : a folder of headers and a CMake package. You do not need the engine's source or its libraries, and any C++17 compiler works (GCC, Clang, MSVC), whichever one built the engine. The game ends up as several source files : scripts that live on actors, a component with a system, and a console variable.

docs.title: What the SDK is, in a few lines
docs.text: Your game is compiled apart from the engine, so the two cannot share C++ objects. They talk through a small set of plain C functions, the C ABI. The C++ SDK is a layer of headers that hides those C functions behind classes and lambdas (Shard::Script, s.Each(...)), so you write ordinary C++ and never call the C functions yourself. It is compiled into your plugin and costs nothing at run time when the code stays simple. You only need to know C++ syntax (classes, templates used as shown, lambdas) to follow this tutorial. The full picture, and what can make a plugin slower, is in The C ABI and the SDK.

docs.title: 1. Get the SDK
docs.text:
From an engine build :

cmake --install build --component sdk --prefix <dir>

The SDK is installed in <dir>/sdk : include/ (the headers), cmake/ (the CMake package), bin/ShardPkg (packs and signs plugins), templates/plugin/ and VERSION. The ShardSDKArchive target puts the same folder in build/shard-sdk-<version>.zip, and the CI publishes one per OS (artifacts shard-sdk-Windows and shard-sdk-Linux). In the engine's repository, the sdk/ folder is already an SDK, without bin/.

docs.title: 2. Start from the template
docs.text:
Copy sdk/templates/plugin to a folder of your own :

my-game/
  CMakeLists.txt        find_package(ShardSDK 1.0) and shard_sdk_add_plugin : rename the target (template_plugin) and the project
  shard-plugin.json     the manifest : change "id" (reverse DNS, lowercase, like com.yourname.mygame)
  src/
    module.cpp          the plugin's entry point : console variables, content, hot reload
    module.hpp          what the files share with it
    gameplay/spinner.*  a script, in a header and a source file
    ecs/drift.cpp       a component and a system
  content/              files the plugin reads through mod://<id>/

Every .cpp under src/ is part of the plugin (SOURCE_DIRS src in the CMakeLists), in whatever folders you put them. To add a feature you add files : the CMakeLists does not list them.

docs.title: 3. Build it
docs.text:
cmake -S my-game -B my-game/build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<dir>/sdk
cmake --build my-game/build

The plugin is written to my-game/build/plugins/<id>/ : the manifest (the SDK adds "abi": "c1" and the path of the library), bin/<platform>/ and content/. The library exports a single symbol, shard_plugin_entry. Built with MinGW it carries its own C++ runtime. Built with MSVC it needs the Visual C++ runtime, like any MSVC program.

docs.title: 4. Load it
docs.text:
Pass the folder to the engine :

ShardHeadless --game <game library> --project <project.json> --plugin my-game/build/plugins/<id> --list-plugins

You can also copy it into the project's plugins folder, where the editor and the player find it. --check-plugins runs the simulation twice, once with one job thread and once with several, and fails if the final state differs. A plugin that affects the simulation has to pass it.

If the engine says built for the C ABI 1.4, this engine has 1.3, it is older than the SDK. Build against an SDK that is not newer than the oldest engine you want to support (see step 9).

In the editor, the script shows up in the Add component menu of the inspector as <id>.Spinner. Add it to an actor and press play.

docs.title: 5. Write a script
docs.text:
A script is a class that lives on an actor. The engine creates it with the component and calls it the way it calls its own scripts. Here is Health, in two files :

// src/gameplay/health.hpp
#pragma once
#include <shard/game.hpp>

class Health : public Shard::Script {
public:
    // Fields : shown in the inspector, saved with the world. Each one is declared where it is, with its options
    SHARD_FIELD(float, maxHealth, Range(1.f, 1000.f), Tooltip("Hit points at the start")) = 100.f;
    SHARD_FIELD(float, current, Runtime()) = 100.f;     // Runtime : shown, not saved
    SHARD_FIELD(Shard::Text, label);                    // a text, edited in the inspector
    float invulnerableFor = 0.f;                        // not a field : a normal member

    void OnPlay() override { current = maxHealth; }
    void OnTick(float deltaTime) override;

    void Damage(float amount) { current -= amount; }
};

// src/gameplay/health.cpp
#include "health.hpp"

void Health::OnTick(float)
{
    if (current <= 0.f) Owner().Destroy();  // destroys the actor, its components and its children. This script gets OnDestroyed
}

SHARD_REGISTER_SCRIPT(Health)

The last line registers the class. Nothing else refers to the file. In the editor the script is the component <id>.Health.

SHARD_FIELD(Type, name, options...) declares the member (the default value goes after it, like for any member) and tells the SDK its name, its type, where it is in the object and its options. The options are Range(min, max), Tooltip("text"), Runtime() (shown and read only, not saved) and Hidden() (neither shown nor saved). Give every field a default : a plain float x; starts at zero while the class has no constructor of its own, and with whatever was in memory otherwise.

A script can override these :

Callback Called OnCreate the script joined an actor that is in a world OnPlay, OnStop play mode starts, stops OnTick(dt) every frame OnFixedTick(dt) every physics step, before the step. Use it for forces and anything that must be reproducible OnLateTick(dt) every frame, after everything has moved. Use it for cameras OnActivated, OnDeactivated, OnDestroyed the script or its actor changes state or is destroyed OnWorldLoaded, OnWorldUnloaded the world finished loading, is about to unload

Members that are not declared with SHARD_FIELD stay out of the inspector and the world file. In a copy of the actor made for play mode they start fresh.

The older way still works : SHARD_REGISTER_SCRIPT(Health, (maxHealth)(current)) lists the members in the .cpp (SHARD_REGISTER_SCRIPT_EX adds options), and the two can be mixed in one class.

docs.title: 6. Talk to the world
docs.text:
A script gets its actor with Owner() and reaches the rest of the world from there :

// src/gameplay/player.cpp
#include "player.hpp"
#include "health.hpp"                       // a script from another file : include its header, nothing to link

void Player::OnTick(float dt)
{
    const float turn = Shard::Input::Axis(Shard::Key::A, Shard::Key::D);
    const float forward = Shard::Input::Axis(Shard::Key::S, Shard::Key::W);
    Owner().Translate(Owner().Forward() * (forward * speed * dt));
    Owner().SetRotation(Shard::AxisAngle({ 0.f, 1.f, 0.f }, -turn * 2.f * dt) * Owner().Rotation());

    Shard::Scene scene = GetScene();                        // the world this actor is in
    if (Shard::Input::WasPressed(Shard::Key::Space)) {
        Shard::Actor bullet = scene.Create("Bullet");
        bullet.SetWorldPose(Owner().WorldPose());
        bullet.Add<Shard::Light>().SetIntensity(3.f);                     // an engine component, as a typed handle
        bullet.AddScript<Bullet>();                                       // a script of this plugin
    }
    if (Shard::Actor enemy = scene.Find("Boss"))
        if (Health* health = enemy.GetScript<Health>())
            health->Damage(10.f);
}

SHARD_REGISTER_SCRIPT(Player)
  • Shard::Actor is a handle. Copy it freely and keep it in a member. Once the actor is destroyed, IsValid() returns false, getters return zeroes and setters do nothing.
  • Pose : Position, Rotation and Scale are relative to the parent. WorldPosition, WorldRotation and WorldPose are in world space. There are also Forward, Right, Up, LookAt and Translate.
